ch1-1.title: 1.1 Number Systems
ch1-1.subtitle: Binary, Hexadecimal, Denary and conversions

keyTerms.name: Binary
keyTerms.def: Base-2 number system using digits 0 and 1.

keyTerms.name: Hexadecimal
keyTerms.def: Base-16 system using digits 0–9 and A–F.

keyTerms.name: Denary / Decimal
keyTerms.def: Base-10 system — the everyday number system.

keyTerms.name: Nibble
keyTerms.def: 4 bits — one hex digit maps to exactly one nibble.

keyTerms.name: Byte
keyTerms.def: 8 bits — two hex digits.

ch1-1.theory:
In binary (base 2), each bit position has a place value that is a power of 2. For an 8-bit number the place values from left (most significant) to right (least significant) are: 128 — 64 — 32 — 16 — 8 — 4 — 2 — 1.

Binary → Denary: Identify which bits are 1 and sum their place values.
Denary → Binary: Repeatedly divide by 2, recording remainders; read remainders bottom-to-top.
Hex → Binary: Replace each hex digit with its 4-bit (nibble) equivalent. A=1010, B=1011, C=1100, D=1101, E=1110, F=1111.
Denary → Hex: Repeatedly divide by 16; remainders ≥ 10 become A–F.

Binary addition rules: 0+0=0  |  0+1=1  |  1+1=10 (0, carry 1)  |  1+1+1=11 (1, carry 1). Overflow occurs when the result exceeds the bit width of the register.
ch1-1.example:
Example 1 — Binary to Denary: Convert 10110101₂

Place values: 128+0+32+16+0+4+0+1 = 181

Example 2 — Denary to Hex: 181 ÷ 16 = 11 remainder 5 → digits are 11 (=B) and 5 → B5₁₆

Example 3 — Hex to Binary: B5 → B=1011, 5=0101 → 1011 0101

ch1-2.title: 1.2 Two's Complement
ch1-2.subtitle: Representing negative integers in binary

keyTerms.name: Two's complement
keyTerms.def: Method to represent negative integers where negation = invert bits + add 1.

keyTerms.name: Sign bit
keyTerms.def: Most significant bit (MSB): 0 = positive, 1 = negative in two's complement.

keyTerms.name: Overflow
keyTerms.def: Result exceeds the representable range for the given bit width.

ch1-2.theory:
To represent a negative number in two's complement:

  • Step 1: Write the magnitude (positive value) in binary.
  • Step 2: Invert all bits (flip every 0 to 1 and every 1 to 0).
  • Step 3: Add 1 to the result.

In 8-bit two's complement the MSB has the weight −128 (not +128). So for a pattern with MSB=1, the value = −128 + (sum of remaining place values).

To decode a negative pattern: invert all bits, add 1, then negate. Overflow in addition: if two positive numbers produce a negative result (MSB becomes 1), overflow has occurred.

questions.stem: Show the 8-bit two's complement representation of −45. Show all three steps of your working.
questions.ms: Step 1: 00101101 [1]; Step 2 invert: 11010010; Step 3 add 1: 11010011 [1 for completing correctly].

questions.stem: State the range of values that can be represented in 8-bit two's complement.
questions.ms: −128 to +127 [1 mark].

questions.stem: Two 8-bit two's complement numbers are added: 01101010 + 00111100.
questions.ms: (a) 10100110 [1]. (b) −90 (two's complement interpretation) [1]. (c) Overflow has occurred — two positive numbers produced a result with MSB=1, which is negative in two's complement [1].

questions.stem: The 8-bit two's complement number 11001010 is stored.
questions.ms: (a) −54 [1]. (b) Any of: single representation of zero [1]; arithmetic works without special cases [1].

ch1-3.title: 1.3 Floating Point
ch1-3.subtitle: Normalised binary floating-point representation

keyTerms.name: Mantissa
keyTerms.def: The significant digits (fractional part) of a floating-point number.

keyTerms.name: Exponent
keyTerms.def: The power of 2 — determines the magnitude of the number.

keyTerms.name: Normalised form
keyTerms.def: Maximises precision: no redundant leading bits in the mantissa.

keyTerms.name: Precision
keyTerms.def: The number of significant bits — determined by mantissa length.

keyTerms.name: Range
keyTerms.def: Largest/smallest representable value — determined by exponent length.

ch1-3.theory:
A floating-point number is stored as: value = mantissa × 2^exponent. Both the mantissa and exponent are stored as two's complement binary.

Normalised form rules:

  • Positive mantissa — starts 0.1... (the bit after the binary point must be 1).
  • Negative mantissa — starts 1.0... (the bit after the binary point must be 0).

Normalisation ensures the maximum number of significant bits are used (no leading redundant 0s or 1s).

Precision vs Range trade-off: More bits for the mantissa → greater precision (more significant digits). More bits for the exponent → wider range (larger/smaller numbers). The two compete for the fixed total bit width.
ch1-3.example:
8-bit mantissa: 0.1101000   4-bit exponent: 0011 (= +3)

Shift the binary point 3 places right: 0.1101000 → 110.1000

Convert 110.1₂: 4 + 2 + 0.5 = 6.5

The mantissa 0.1101000 is normalised because it starts 0.1 (positive form).

questions.stem: Explain what it means for a positive floating-point number to be in normalised form. State the condition for a normalised negative floating-point number.
questions.ms: Positive: mantissa starts 0.1... — the bit after the binary point is 1 [1]. Negative: mantissa starts 1.0... — the bit after the binary point is 0 [1].

questions.stem: A floating-point number uses an 8-bit normalised mantissa and a 4-bit two's complement exponent. Mantissa = 0.1101000, Exponent = 0011. Calculate the denary value. Show your working.
questions.ms: Exponent = 3 [1]. Shift binary point 3 right → 110.1000 [1]. Value = 4 + 2 + 0.5 = 6.5 [1].

questions.stem: A computer stores floating-point numbers using 32 bits total. A programmer increases the mantissa from 23 bits to 27 bits (reducing the exponent from 8 to 4 bits). State the effect on:
questions.ms: (a) Precision increases — more significant bits available [1]. (b) Range decreases — fewer exponent bits mean a smaller maximum value [1].

questions.stem: Explain why floating-point arithmetic can produce rounding errors.
questions.ms: Any two of: some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary [1]; converting to/from normalised form may discard bits [1]; limited mantissa bits means some values must be approximated [1].

ch1-4.title: 1.4 BCD
ch1-4.subtitle: Binary Coded Decimal

keyTerms.name: BCD
keyTerms.def: Binary Coded Decimal — each decimal digit stored as a separate 4-bit binary value.

keyTerms.name: Packed BCD
keyTerms.def: Two BCD digits stored per byte, using both nibbles.

keyTerms.name: Invalid patterns
keyTerms.def: Bit patterns 1010–1111 (10–15) are unused/invalid in BCD.

ch1-4.theory:
In BCD, each decimal digit (0–9) is encoded individually as a 4-bit binary value (0000–1001). Bit patterns 1010 to 1111 are invalid in BCD.

Example: 79 in BCD = 0111 1001 (7=0111, 9=1001).

Where it is used: calculators, digital clocks, financial systems — anywhere exact decimal representation matters and decimal-to-binary conversion errors must be avoided.

Disadvantage: less efficient than pure binary. For example, 99 needs 8 bits in BCD but only 7 bits in standard binary. Packed BCD improves storage by fitting two digits into one byte.
ch1-4.example:
Convert 94 to BCD: 9 = 1001, 4 = 0100 → BCD = 1001 0100

Convert BCD 0011 0111 to decimal: 0011 = 3, 0111 = 7 → decimal 37

questions.stem: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using BCD rather than standard binary to store numbers.
questions.ms: Advantage: easy conversion to decimal display / no rounding errors for decimal fractions [1]. Disadvantage: less efficient use of bits / some bit patterns wasted [1].

questions.stem: A calculator stores monetary values using BCD. Explain why BCD is more suitable than standard binary for this purpose.
questions.ms: BCD can represent exact decimal values without conversion errors / each digit maps directly to a display digit without conversion [1].

ch1-5.title: 1.5 Character Encoding
ch1-5.subtitle: ASCII, Extended ASCII and Unicode (UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32)

keyTerms.name: ASCII
keyTerms.def: 7-bit standard — 128 characters covering basic English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes.

keyTerms.name: Extended ASCII
keyTerms.def: 8-bit extension — 256 characters; varies by platform/code page.

keyTerms.name: Unicode
keyTerms.def: International standard assigning a unique code point to every character in every writing system (140,000+ characters).

keyTerms.name: UTF-8
keyTerms.def: Variable-width encoding: 1 byte for ASCII range, 2–4 bytes for others. Backwards-compatible with ASCII.

keyTerms.name: UTF-16
keyTerms.def: Uses 2 bytes for most common characters, 4 bytes for others.

keyTerms.name: UTF-32
keyTerms.def: Fixed 4 bytes per character — simple indexing but wastes space for English text.

ch1-5.theory:
ASCII covers basic English characters and control codes using 7 bits per character. Extended ASCII adds characters 128–255 but implementations vary by platform.

Unicode was introduced to support all world languages. It assigns a unique code point (e.g. U+0041 = 'A') to every character in every writing system.

UTF-8 uses 1 byte for the ASCII range (0–127), making it backwards-compatible. Characters above 127 use 2–4 bytes. It is the most common encoding on the web and is most efficient for English text.

UTF-32 always uses 4 bytes per character. Its fixed width makes string indexing trivial but it wastes space — an English document in UTF-32 is 4× larger than in ASCII.
ch1-5.example:
ASCII 'A' = 65 decimal = 0100 0001 binary. 'B'=66, 'Z'=90, 'a'=97.

The difference between upper and lower case is always 32 (bit 5 is toggled).

A file with 500 ASCII characters = 500 bytes. The same file in UTF-32 = 500 × 4 = 2,000 bytes.

questions.stem: The ASCII code for 'A' is 65. State the ASCII code for 'E'.
questions.ms: 69 [1].

questions.stem: Explain why Unicode was introduced when ASCII already existed.
questions.ms: Any two of: ASCII only covers English/Western characters [1]; Unicode provides a unique code point for every character in all world languages/scripts [1]; needed for international software and the web [1].

questions.stem: A document contains 800 characters. Calculate the file size in bytes if encoded using:
questions.ms: (a) 800 × 1 = 800 bytes [1]. (b) 800 × 4 = 3200 bytes [1].

questions.stem: State one advantage of UTF-8 over UTF-32 for storing English text. State one advantage of UTF-32 over UTF-8.
questions.ms: UTF-8 advantage: uses only 1 byte per ASCII character — much smaller file size for English text [1]. UTF-32 advantage: fixed width makes it easier to index into a string / simpler character-position arithmetic [1].

ch1-6.title: 1.6 Images & Sound
ch1-6.subtitle: Bitmap graphics and digital audio representation

keyTerms.name: Pixel
keyTerms.def: The smallest addressable element in a bitmap image.

keyTerms.name: Colour depth
keyTerms.def: Bits per pixel — determines the number of possible colours (2^depth).

keyTerms.name: Resolution
keyTerms.def: Width × height in pixels, or pixels per inch (PPI).

keyTerms.name: Sample rate
keyTerms.def: Number of amplitude measurements per second (Hz) in digital audio.

keyTerms.name: Bit depth
keyTerms.def: Bits per audio sample — determines amplitude precision.

keyTerms.name: ADC
keyTerms.def: Analogue-to-Digital Converter — samples and quantises an analogue signal.

keyTerms.name: Nyquist theorem
keyTerms.def: Sample rate must be ≥ 2× the highest frequency to avoid aliasing.

keyTerms.name: Aliasing
keyTerms.def: Distortion caused by undersampling — high frequencies appear as lower ones.

ch1-6.theory:
Bitmap images: A bitmap is a grid of pixels. Each pixel is stored as a binary value.

  • Colour depth 1-bit = black & white (2 colours)
  • 8-bit = 256 colours
  • 24-bit = 16,777,216 colours (TrueColour)

Image file size (bits) = width (px) × height (px) × colour depth (bits per pixel). Divide by 8 for bytes, by 1024 for KB, by 1024² for MB.

Digital sound: Analogue sound is captured by an ADC. The ADC measures the amplitude of the sound wave at regular intervals (the sample rate) and records each measurement as a binary value (bit depth).

Sound file size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration (seconds) × number of channels.

Nyquist theorem: to accurately reproduce a frequency, the sample rate must be at least twice that frequency. CD audio uses 44,100 Hz to cover up to ~22,050 Hz (beyond human hearing).
ch1-6.example:
Image example: 640 × 480 pixels, 24-bit colour.

Size = 640 × 480 × 24 = 7,372,800 bits ÷ 8 = 921,600 bytes = 900 KB

Sound example: 44,100 Hz, 16-bit, mono, 10 seconds.

Size = 44,100 × 16 × 10 × 1 = 7,056,000 bits ÷ 8 = 882,000 bytes ≈ 861 KB

questions.stem: A bitmap image is 1024 pixels wide and 768 pixels high with a colour depth of 24 bits per pixel. Calculate the file size in kilobytes. Show your working.
A sound clip is recorded at 44,100 Hz sample rate, 16-bit depth, stereo (2 channels), for 30 seconds. Calculate the file size in megabytes. Show your working.
Explain the effect of (a) increasing the sample rate and (b) increasing the bit depth on a digital sound recording.
questions.ms: (a) More samples per second → higher frequencies reproduced more accurately → better quality but larger file size [1]. (b) More bits per sample → finer amplitude resolution → less quantisation noise but larger file size [1].

questions.stem: State what the Nyquist theorem says and explain what aliasing is.
questions.ms: Nyquist: the sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal [1]. Aliasing: if the sample rate is too low, high frequencies are misrepresented as lower frequencies [1].

ch1-7.title: 1.7 Compression
ch1-7.subtitle: Lossy, lossless, RLE and Huffman coding

keyTerms.name: Lossy compression
keyTerms.def: Permanently removes data — quality is reduced irreversibly (e.g. JPEG, MP3).

keyTerms.name: Lossless compression
keyTerms.def: Data can be perfectly reconstructed — no information is lost (e.g. PNG, ZIP).

keyTerms.name: Run-Length Encoding (RLE)
keyTerms.def: Replaces runs of identical values with a (count, value) pair.

keyTerms.name: Huffman coding
keyTerms.def: Variable-length codes — more frequent symbols receive shorter bit codes.

ch1-7.theory:
Lossy compression (JPEG, MP3, AAC) removes information that is less perceptible to humans. It achieves much smaller file sizes but the original cannot be recovered. Suitable for photos, music, and video.

Lossless compression (PNG, GIF, ZIP, FLAC) allows exact reconstruction of the original data. Required for text files, executable programs, medical images, and financial data.

Run-Length Encoding (RLE): Scans data and replaces consecutive repeated values with a (count, value) pair. Highly effective for simple graphics with large uniform areas.

Huffman coding: Builds a frequency tree from symbol frequencies. The most common symbol receives the shortest bit code. This reduces the average number of bits per symbol below the fixed-width encoding.
ch1-7.example:
RLE example: Row WWWWWBBBWW → 5W 3B 2W (3 pairs instead of 10 values — saves 7 values).

Huffman example: A=50%, B=25%, C=15%, D=10% → codes: A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111.

Message AABAC = 0 0 10 0 110 = 7 bits. Fixed 2-bit codes: 5 × 2 = 10 bits. Saving: 3 bits.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression. Give one example of each.
questions.ms: Lossy: permanently removes data / quality cannot be recovered [1] e.g. JPEG / MP3. Lossless: data can be exactly restored [1] e.g. PNG / ZIP / RLE / FLAC.

questions.stem: Using run-length encoding, compress the following data: AAAAAABBBBAACCCC. Show the compressed form and state the number of values stored before and after.
questions.ms: Compressed: 6A 4B 2A 4C [1]. Before: 16 values [1]. After: 8 values (4 pairs) [1].

questions.stem: A Huffman encoding scheme assigns: A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111. The original message is AABCAD.
questions.ms: (a) A=0, A=0, B=10, C=110, A=0, D=111 → 00 10 110 0 111 = 10 bits [2]. (b) 6 × 2 = 12 bits [1]. (c) 12 − 10 = 2 bits saved [1].

questions.stem: State two situations where lossless compression must be used instead of lossy compression.
questions.ms: Any two of: executable / program files [1]; text documents [1]; medical or scientific data [1]; financial records [1]; database files [1].

ch11-1.title: 12.1 Variables & Types
ch11-1.subtitle: DECLARE, data types and constants in Cambridge pseudocode

keyTerms.name: DECLARE
keyTerms.def: Pseudocode keyword used to create a variable: DECLARE x : INTEGER

keyTerms.name: INTEGER
keyTerms.def: Whole number data type (positive or negative, no decimal point).

keyTerms.name: REAL
keyTerms.def: Decimal/floating-point number data type.

keyTerms.name: BOOLEAN
keyTerms.def: Two-state data type: TRUE or FALSE.

keyTerms.name: CONSTANT
keyTerms.def: An identifier whose value cannot change during execution. CONSTANT Pi ← 3.14159

keyTerms.name: Assignment (←)
keyTerms.def: Stores a value into a variable. x ← 10 puts the value 10 into x.

ch11-1.theory:
📚 Langfield & Duddell — Ch. 14
"Most programming languages require you to declare the type of data to be stored in a variable, so the correct amount of memory space can be reserved. A variable declared to store a whole number (INTEGER) cannot then be used to store alphanumeric characters (STRING). It is good programming practice to include a comment about the variables you are planning to use and the type of data you will store in them."

In Cambridge 9618 pseudocode every variable must be declared before use with the keyword DECLARE, followed by its identifier and data type:

DECLARE age      : INTEGER
DECLARE price    : REAL
DECLARE initial  : CHAR
DECLARE name     : STRING
DECLARE isPassed : BOOLEAN

Assignment uses the left-arrow operator ←. The right-hand side is evaluated first, then stored:

age ← 17
price ← 4.99
isPassed ← TRUE

Constants are declared with CONSTANT and cannot be reassigned. Using constants makes programs easier to maintain — change the value in one place.

Type rules: you cannot assign a REAL value to an INTEGER variable without explicit conversion. String concatenation uses the & operator: "Hello" & " World".
ch11-1.example:
Worked example — temperature converter:

DECLARE celsius    : REAL
DECLARE fahrenheit : REAL
CONSTANT freezing  ← 32

celsius ← 100
fahrenheit ← celsius * 1.8 + freezing
OUTPUT fahrenheit   // outputs 212

Note: CONSTANT is declared without a type keyword — Cambridge pseudocode infers the type from the value.

ch11-2.title: 12.2 Selection
ch11-2.subtitle: IF…THEN…ELSE and CASE…OF in Cambridge pseudocode

keyTerms.name: IF…THEN…ELSE…ENDIF
keyTerms.def: Conditional branching: executes one block if condition is TRUE, another if FALSE.

keyTerms.name: CASE OF…OTHERWISE…ENDCASE
keyTerms.def: Multi-way selection: matches a variable against several possible values.

keyTerms.name: Condition
keyTerms.def: A Boolean expression that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE (e.g. x > 5).

keyTerms.name: Nested IF
keyTerms.def: An IF statement placed inside another IF block to test multiple conditions.

ch11-2.theory:
IF statement syntax:

IF condition
  THEN
    // statements if TRUE
  ELSE
    // statements if FALSE
ENDIF

The ELSE branch is optional. For multiple conditions use ELSE IF (nested) or CASE OF.

CASE OF syntax — used when one variable is tested against several discrete values:

CASE OF grade
  'A' : OUTPUT "Distinction"
  'B' : OUTPUT "Merit"
  'C' : OUTPUT "Pass"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Fail"
ENDCASE

Cambridge examiners expect correct keywords and indentation. ENDCASE and ENDIF are mandatory closing keywords.
ch11-2.example:
Example — grade boundaries:

DECLARE mark : INTEGER
mark ← 72
IF mark >= 70
  THEN OUTPUT "Distinction"
  ELSE
    IF mark >= 50
      THEN OUTPUT "Pass"
      ELSE OUTPUT "Fail"
    ENDIF
ENDIF

questions.ms: IF age >= 18 [1] THEN OUTPUT "Adult" [1] ELSE OUTPUT "Minor" ENDIF [1].

questions.stem: State one advantage of using CASE OF instead of nested IF statements.
questions.ms: More readable / easier to follow when testing one variable against many values [1].

ch11-3.title: 12.3 Iteration
ch11-3.subtitle: FOR, WHILE and REPEAT…UNTIL loops

keyTerms.name: FOR…TO…NEXT
keyTerms.def: Count-controlled loop: runs a fixed number of times with a counter variable.

keyTerms.name: WHILE…DO…ENDWHILE
keyTerms.def: Pre-condition loop: checks the condition before each iteration; may run 0 times.

keyTerms.name: REPEAT…UNTIL
keyTerms.def: Post-condition loop: always runs at least once; condition checked at the end.

keyTerms.name: Iteration
keyTerms.def: Repeated execution of a block of statements.

ch11-3.theory:
FOR loop — use when the number of iterations is known:

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  OUTPUT i
NEXT i

WHILE loop — use when the number of iterations is unknown but a pre-check is needed:

WHILE count > 0 DO
  count ← count - 1
ENDWHILE

REPEAT…UNTIL — use when the loop body must run at least once (e.g. input validation):

REPEAT
  OUTPUT "Enter a positive number: "
  INPUT num
UNTIL num > 0

Key difference: WHILE checks the condition before the body; REPEAT checks it after.
ch11-3.example:
Calculating a sum with FOR:

DECLARE total : INTEGER
DECLARE i     : INTEGER
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
  total ← total + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT total   // 15

questions.ms: REPEAT…UNTIL [1]; because the input must be read at least once before the condition can be checked [1].

ch11-4.title: 12.4 Procedures & Functions
ch11-4.subtitle: Defining and calling procedures and functions with parameters

keyTerms.name: PROCEDURE
keyTerms.def: A named subroutine that performs a task but does not return a value.

keyTerms.name: FUNCTION
keyTerms.def: A named subroutine that performs a task AND returns a single value.

keyTerms.name: RETURNS
keyTerms.def: Keyword in a FUNCTION header specifying the data type of the returned value.

keyTerms.name: CALL
keyTerms.def: Keyword used to invoke a PROCEDURE: CALL PrintName("Alice").

keyTerms.name: Parameter
keyTerms.def: A variable listed in the subroutine header that receives a value when called.

keyTerms.name: Argument
keyTerms.def: The actual value passed to a subroutine when it is called.

ch11-4.theory:
Procedure syntax:

PROCEDURE Greet(name : STRING)
  OUTPUT "Hello, " & name
ENDPROCEDURE

CALL Greet("Alice")

Function syntax:

FUNCTION Square(n : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN n * n
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT Square(5)   // 25

Key rules: Functions must include RETURNS type in the header and use RETURN value in the body. Procedures use CALL but functions are called directly in an expression. Both use local variables that cease to exist after the subroutine ends.
ch11-4.example:
Function returning the maximum of two numbers:

FUNCTION Maximum(a : INTEGER, b : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  IF a > b
    THEN RETURN a
    ELSE RETURN b
  ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT Maximum(7, 3)   // 7

questions.stem: State two differences between a procedure and a function in Cambridge pseudocode.
questions.ms: A function returns a value; a procedure does not [1]. A procedure is called with CALL; a function is used directly in an expression [1].

questions.stem: Write a FUNCTION IsEven that takes an INTEGER parameter n and returns TRUE if n is even, FALSE otherwise.
questions.ms: FUNCTION IsEven(n : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN [1]; IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN RETURN TRUE ELSE RETURN FALSE ENDIF [1]; ENDFUNCTION [1].

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by a "local variable" and why local variables are important in subroutines.
questions.ms: A local variable exists only within the subroutine where it is declared [1]. It prevents naming conflicts and side-effects in other parts of the program [1].

ch11-5.title: 12.5 Arrays
ch11-5.subtitle: 1D and 2D array declaration, access and traversal

keyTerms.name: Array
keyTerms.def: A fixed-size, ordered collection of elements of the same data type.

keyTerms.name: 1D array
keyTerms.def: A single row of elements accessed by one index: scores[3].

keyTerms.name: 2D array
keyTerms.def: A table of elements accessed by row and column: grid[2,4].

keyTerms.name: Index
keyTerms.def: The position of an element in an array. Cambridge pseudocode uses 1-based indexing by default.

keyTerms.name: DECLARE (array)
keyTerms.def: DECLARE scores : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER declares a 5-element integer array.

ch11-5.theory:
1D array declaration and access:

DECLARE scores : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
scores[1] ← 88
scores[2] ← 72
OUTPUT scores[1]   // 88

2D array:

DECLARE grid : ARRAY[1:3, 1:3] OF INTEGER
grid[2,3] ← 7

Traversing with a loop:

DECLARE i : INTEGER
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
  OUTPUT scores[i]
NEXT i

Arrays have a fixed size declared at compile time — you cannot resize them during execution.
ch11-5.example:
Find the maximum in an array:

DECLARE nums : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
DECLARE max  : INTEGER
DECLARE i    : INTEGER
nums[1]←3; nums[2]←9; nums[3]←1; nums[4]←7; nums[5]←5
max ← nums[1]
FOR i ← 2 TO 5
  IF nums[i] > max THEN max ← nums[i] ENDIF
NEXT i
OUTPUT max   // 9

questions.stem: Write pseudocode to declare a 1D array temps that can hold 7 REAL values, then assign the value 36.6 to the third element.
questions.ms: DECLARE temps : ARRAY[1:7] OF REAL [1]; temps[3] ← 36.6 [1].

questions.stem: A 2D array is declared as ARRAY[1:4, 1:3]. State (a) the number of rows, (b) the number of columns, (c) the total number of elements.
Write pseudocode to calculate the sum of all elements in a 1D INTEGER array data with indices 1 to 6.
questions.ms: DECLARE total, i : INTEGER; total ← 0 [1]; FOR i ← 1 TO 6 [1]; total ← total + data[i]; NEXT i; OUTPUT total [1].

ch11-6.title: 12.6 String Handling
ch11-6.subtitle: Built-in string functions: LENGTH, SUBSTRING, LCASE, UCASE, MID

keyTerms.name: LENGTH(s)
keyTerms.def: Returns the number of characters in string s.

keyTerms.name: SUBSTRING(s, start, len)
keyTerms.def: Returns len characters from string s beginning at position start (1-based).

keyTerms.name: UCASE(s) / LCASE(s)
keyTerms.def: Converts all characters in s to upper or lower case.

keyTerms.name: Concatenation (&)
keyTerms.def: Joins two strings: "Hello" & " World" → "Hello World".

keyTerms.name: String index
keyTerms.def: Cambridge pseudocode strings are 1-indexed: the first character is at position 1.

ch11-6.theory:
Cambridge pseudocode provides several built-in functions for string manipulation:

FunctionExampleResult
LENGTH(s)LENGTH("Hello")5
SUBSTRING(s,p,n)SUBSTRING("Hello",2,3)"ell"
UCASE(s)UCASE("hello")"HELLO"
LCASE(s)LCASE("HeLLo")"hello"

To extract the first character: SUBSTRING(s, 1, 1). To extract the last character: SUBSTRING(s, LENGTH(s), 1).
ch11-6.example:
Capitalise the first letter of a name:

DECLARE name   : STRING
DECLARE result : STRING
name ← "alice"
result ← UCASE(SUBSTRING(name, 1, 1)) & SUBSTRING(name, 2, LENGTH(name) - 1)
OUTPUT result   // "Alice"

questions.stem: A variable word holds the string "Cambridge". State the result of: (a) LENGTH(word)   (b) SUBSTRING(word, 1, 3)   (c) LCASE(word)
Write pseudocode to read a string from the user and output the last three characters of the string.
questions.ms: INPUT s [1]; OUTPUT SUBSTRING(s, LENGTH(s) - 2, 3) [2] — award 1 for SUBSTRING attempt, 1 for correct length calculation.

questions.stem: Explain why string comparison in pseudocode is case-sensitive and how you would overcome this when checking if a user typed "yes".
questions.ms: Strings compare character by character using ASCII/Unicode values; "Yes" ≠ "yes" [1]. Convert input to lower case first: IF LCASE(answer) = "yes" [1].

ch12-1.title: 13.1 Program Design
ch12-1.subtitle: Top-down design, structure charts and stepwise refinement

keyTerms.name: Top-down design
keyTerms.def: Breaking a large problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems.

keyTerms.name: Stepwise refinement
keyTerms.def: Repeatedly decomposing each sub-problem until modules are simple enough to code.

keyTerms.name: Structure chart
keyTerms.def: A hierarchy diagram showing how a program is divided into modules and how they communicate via parameters.

keyTerms.name: Module
keyTerms.def: A self-contained unit of code (procedure or function) with a single purpose.

keyTerms.name: Cohesion
keyTerms.def: How focused a module is on a single task. High cohesion is desirable.

keyTerms.name: Coupling
keyTerms.def: The degree of dependency between modules. Low coupling is desirable.

ch12-1.theory:
📚 Langfield & Duddell — Ch. 15.02
"An alternative approach to modular design is to choose sub-tasks and construct a structure chart to show the interrelations between modules. Each box represents a module. Each level is a refinement of the level above. The chart also shows the interface between modules — variables referred to as 'parameters'. A parameter supplying a value downward is shown as a downwards-pointing arrow; one supplying a value upward is shown as an upward-pointing arrow. A diamond shape shows a condition (True/False). A semi-circular arrow represents repetition."

Top-down design starts with the whole system and decomposes it level by level. Each level adds more detail. The result is a hierarchy of modules, each responsible for one aspect of the program.

Structure charts represent this hierarchy visually:

  • Boxes = modules (procedures/functions)
  • Arrows down = calls
  • Small arrow on connecting line = data passed as a parameter
  • Diamond on connecting line = flag/condition parameter
  • Loop arc = repeated call (iteration)

Structure charts are not flowcharts — they show what is called and what data is passed, not how decisions are made inside a module.

Benefits: easier to test each module in isolation; teams can work on separate modules; modules can be reused.
ch12-1.example:
Student grade system — partial structure chart description:

Top-level: Process Student Grades
Level 2: Read Data | Calculate Average | Output Results
Calculate Average calls Sum Scores (passes: scores array → receives: total)

questions.stem: Describe what is meant by "top-down design" and state two benefits of this approach.
questions.ms: Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems recursively [1]. Benefits (any two): modules can be tested independently [1]; easier to divide work between programmers [1]; modules may be reused [1].

questions.stem: On a structure chart, what does a small arrow on a connecting line between two boxes represent?
questions.ms: A data item (parameter) being passed between the calling module and the called module [1].

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a structure chart and a flowchart.
questions.ms: A structure chart shows the hierarchy of modules and the data passed between them [1]. A flowchart shows the sequence of steps and decisions within a single algorithm/module [1].

ch12-2.title: 13.2 Structured Programming
ch12-2.subtitle: Sequence, selection, iteration; programming style and maintainability

keyTerms.name: Sequence
keyTerms.def: Statements executed one after another in the order they appear.

keyTerms.name: Selection
keyTerms.def: A branching construct (IF/CASE) that chooses which block to execute.

keyTerms.name: Iteration
keyTerms.def: A looping construct (FOR/WHILE/REPEAT) that repeats a block.

keyTerms.name: Structured programming
keyTerms.def: A style that uses only sequence, selection and iteration — no GOTO statements.

keyTerms.name: Identifier naming
keyTerms.def: Meaningful variable and procedure names improve readability: totalScore not ts.

ch12-2.theory:
Structured programming, proposed by Dijkstra, limits programs to three constructs — sequence, selection, iteration — avoiding GOTO. This produces programs that are easier to read, test and maintain.

Good programming style in Cambridge 9618:

  • Meaningful identifiers: studentAge not x
  • Constants for magic numbers: CONSTANT MaxSize ← 100
  • Comments: use // to explain non-obvious logic
  • Indentation: each level of nesting indented consistently
  • One task per subroutine: high cohesion

Programs written in good style are maintainable — other programmers can understand and modify them without introducing new bugs.
ch12-2.example:
Poor style vs good style:

// Poor
x ← 3.14159 * r * r

// Good
CONSTANT PI ← 3.14159
// Calculate the area of a circle with radius r
area ← PI * r * r

questions.stem: Name the three constructs used in structured programming and give a Cambridge pseudocode example of each.
questions.ms: Sequence (e.g. x ← 5) [1]; selection (e.g. IF x > 0) [1]; iteration (e.g. FOR i ← 1 TO 5) [1].

questions.stem: Explain why using meaningful identifier names is important in a large programming project.
questions.ms: Makes the purpose of each variable/procedure clear without needing extra comments [1]; reduces time for other programmers to understand the code, making maintenance easier [1].

questions.stem: State two features of good programming style, other than meaningful identifier names.
questions.ms: Any two: use of constants instead of magic numbers [1]; appropriate comments [1]; consistent indentation [1]; short subroutines with a single purpose [1].

ch12-3.title: 13.3 Parameter Passing (BYVAL / BYREF)
ch12-3.subtitle: Passing parameters by value vs by reference

keyTerms.name: BYVALUE (BYVAL)
keyTerms.def: A copy of the argument is passed; changes inside the subroutine do NOT affect the original variable.

keyTerms.name: BYREFERENCE (BYREF)
keyTerms.def: The memory address of the argument is passed; changes inside the subroutine DO affect the original variable.

keyTerms.name: Formal parameter
keyTerms.def: The parameter name used in the subroutine definition.

keyTerms.name: Actual parameter
keyTerms.def: The value or variable passed in the subroutine call.

ch12-3.theory:
When a subroutine is called, arguments are passed to parameters. Cambridge 9618 supports two mechanisms:

BYVALUE: A copy is made. The original remains unchanged.

PROCEDURE Double(BYVALUE n : INTEGER)
  n ← n * 2
  OUTPUT n       // outputs doubled value
ENDPROCEDURE
DECLARE x : INTEGER
x ← 5
CALL Double(x)
OUTPUT x        // still 5 — original unchanged

BYREFERENCE: The address is passed. Changes affect the original.

PROCEDURE Double(BYREF n : INTEGER)
  n ← n * 2
ENDPROCEDURE
x ← 5
CALL Double(x)
OUTPUT x        // now 10

Use BYREF when a subroutine needs to modify a caller's variable. Use BYVAL to protect against unintended side-effects.
ch12-3.example:
Swap procedure requires BYREF:

PROCEDURE Swap(BYREF a : INTEGER, BYREF b : INTEGER)
  DECLARE temp : INTEGER
  temp ← a
  a ← b
  b ← temp
ENDPROCEDURE

If BYVALUE were used here, a and b inside Swap would be copies — the caller's variables would not be swapped.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between passing a parameter BYVALUE and BYREFERENCE.
questions.ms: BYVALUE: a copy is passed; changes inside the subroutine do not affect the original [1]. BYREFERENCE: the address is passed; changes inside the subroutine do affect the original variable [1].

questions.stem: A procedure increments a counter variable. Should the parameter be passed BYVAL or BYREF? Justify your answer.
questions.ms: BYREF [1]; because the procedure needs to modify the original counter variable in the calling program [1].

questions.stem:
Trace the following pseudocode and state the output:
PROCEDURE Add10(BYVALUE n : INTEGER)
  n ← n + 10
  OUTPUT n
ENDPROCEDURE
DECLARE y : INTEGER
y ← 7
CALL Add10(y)
OUTPUT y
questions.ms: First OUTPUT: 17 [1]; second OUTPUT: 7 (original unchanged because BYVALUE) [1].

ch12-4.title: 13.4 Testing & Debugging
ch12-4.subtitle: Test data categories, trace tables, white-box and black-box testing

keyTerms.name: Normal test data
keyTerms.def: Valid data that the program should accept and process correctly.

keyTerms.name: Boundary test data
keyTerms.def: Data at the exact edge of valid/invalid ranges (e.g. 0 and 100 for a 0–100 range).

keyTerms.name: Erroneous test data
keyTerms.def: Invalid data the program should reject (wrong type, out of range).

keyTerms.name: Trace table
keyTerms.def: A table used to manually track variable values step by step through code.

keyTerms.name: White-box testing
keyTerms.def: Testing with knowledge of the internal code structure; aims to cover all paths.

keyTerms.name: Black-box testing
keyTerms.def: Testing based only on inputs and expected outputs, without seeing the code.

ch12-4.theory:
Testing verifies that a program behaves correctly. Cambridge 9618 expects you to design test data and complete trace tables.

Test data categories:

  • Normal: typical valid input (e.g. age = 25 for a 0–120 range)
  • Boundary: at the boundary of valid input (e.g. age = 0 and age = 120)
  • Erroneous: invalid input the program must reject (e.g. age = -5, age = "abc")

Trace tables have one column per variable and one row per step. You update each cell when a variable changes.

White-box (structural) testing ensures every line and branch is executed at least once. Black-box (functional) testing only looks at what comes out for given inputs.
ch12-4.example:
Trace table for:

x ← 3; y ← 0
WHILE x > 0 DO
  y ← y + x
  x ← x - 1
ENDWHILE
xy
30
23
15
06

questions.stem: A program accepts a mark between 0 and 100 inclusive. Give one example of each: (a) normal data, (b) boundary data, (c) erroneous data.
questions.ms: (a) Any value 1–99, e.g. 55 [1]. (b) 0 or 100 [1]. (c) Any value outside 0–100 or non-numeric, e.g. -1 or "abc" [1].

questions.stem: State one advantage of black-box testing over white-box testing.
questions.ms: The tester does not need to understand the internal code / tests can be written from the specification before coding begins [1].

questions.stem:
Complete a trace table for the following, tracking variables i and total:
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 3
  total ← total + i * i
NEXT i

ch13-1.title: 14.1 Stacks
ch13-1.subtitle: Stack ADT: PUSH, POP, stack pointer, overflow and underflow

keyTerms.name: Stack
keyTerms.def: A LIFO (Last In First Out) abstract data type — the last item pushed is the first item popped.

keyTerms.name: PUSH
keyTerms.def: Add an item to the top of the stack.

keyTerms.name: POP
keyTerms.def: Remove and return the item at the top of the stack.

keyTerms.name: Stack pointer (SP)
keyTerms.def: An integer that points to the index of the current top element.

keyTerms.name: Stack overflow
keyTerms.def: Attempting to PUSH onto a full stack — error condition.

keyTerms.name: Stack underflow
keyTerms.def: Attempting to POP from an empty stack — error condition.

ch13-1.theory:
📚 Langfield & Duddell — Ch. 13.08
"The BaseOfStackPointer always points to the first slot. The TopOfStackPointer points to the last element pushed (added). When an element is popped (removed), TopOfStackPointer decreases to point to the element now at the top. When the stack is empty, TopOfStackPointer has the value −1."

A stack stores items in LIFO order. Implemented as an array with a stack pointer:

DECLARE stack : ARRAY[1:MaxSize] OF INTEGER
DECLARE sp    : INTEGER   // stack pointer; 0 = empty

PROCEDURE Push(item : INTEGER)
  IF sp = MaxSize
    THEN OUTPUT "Stack overflow"
    ELSE sp ← sp + 1
         stack[sp] ← item
  ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION Pop() RETURNS INTEGER
  IF sp = 0
    THEN OUTPUT "Stack underflow"; RETURN -1
    ELSE sp ← sp - 1
         RETURN stack[sp + 1]
  ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

Applications: call stack (subroutine return addresses), undo operations, expression evaluation, depth-first search.
ch13-1.example:
Push 3, 7, 2 then Pop once:

After Push(3): stack=[3], sp=1
After Push(7): stack=[3,7], sp=2
After Push(2): stack=[3,7,2], sp=3
After Pop(): returns 2, sp=2, stack=[3,7]

questions.stem: A stack contains the values [10, 20, 30] with 30 at the top (sp=3). Trace the operations: PUSH(40), POP(), POP(). State the final stack contents and sp.
questions.ms: After PUSH(40): [10,20,30,40] sp=4 [1]; after POP(): returns 40, sp=3 [1]; after POP(): returns 30, sp=2, final stack [10,20] [1].

questions.stem: Explain what "stack overflow" means and state one real situation that can cause it in a running program.
questions.ms: Stack overflow occurs when a PUSH is attempted on a full stack [1]. Infinite/runaway recursion can overflow the call stack [1].

questions.stem: State two applications of stacks in computer systems.
questions.ms: Any two: subroutine call/return addresses [1]; undo functionality in software [1]; expression evaluation / bracket matching [1]; browser back button [1].

ch13-2.title: 14.2 Queues
ch13-2.subtitle: Queue ADT: ENQUEUE, DEQUEUE, front/rear pointers, circular queue

keyTerms.name: Queue
keyTerms.def: A FIFO (First In First Out) abstract data type — the first item added is the first removed.

keyTerms.name: ENQUEUE
keyTerms.def: Add an item to the rear of the queue.

keyTerms.name: DEQUEUE
keyTerms.def: Remove and return the item at the front of the queue.

keyTerms.name: Circular queue
keyTerms.def: An array-based queue where the rear pointer wraps around to index 1 after reaching MaxSize, reusing freed space.

keyTerms.name: Queue overflow/underflow
keyTerms.def: Adding to a full queue or removing from an empty queue — both are error conditions.

ch13-2.theory:
📚 Langfield & Duddell — Ch. 13.09
"When people form a queue, they join the queue at the end and leave from the front. In an orderly queue, no-one pushes in between. A more efficient way to make use of slots is the concept of a 'circular' queue — pointers show where the front and end are and the queue can 'wrap around' to the beginning."

A queue uses two pointers: front and rear. Items enter at the rear and leave from the front.

In a linear queue (simple array), space at the front cannot be reused after dequeuing. A circular queue solves this by wrapping the rear pointer:

// Circular enqueue
IF size = MaxSize
  THEN OUTPUT "Queue full"
  ELSE rear ← (rear MOD MaxSize) + 1
       queue[rear] ← item
       size ← size + 1
ENDIF

Applications: CPU job scheduling, print queues, breadth-first search, network packet buffers.
ch13-2.example:
Circular queue with MaxSize=4:

ENQUEUE A: front=1 rear=1 [A, _, _, _]
ENQUEUE B: rear=2 [A, B, _, _]
DEQUEUE: returns A, front=2 [_, B, _, _]
ENQUEUE C,D,E: rear wraps — C at 3, D at 4, E at 1 (reuses slot)

questions.stem: State the difference between a stack and a queue in terms of the order items are removed.
questions.ms: A stack is LIFO — last item added is the first removed [1]. A queue is FIFO — first item added is the first removed [1].

questions.stem: Explain why a circular queue is preferred over a linear queue when implemented as a fixed-size array.
questions.ms: In a linear queue, dequeued positions at the front cannot be reused, so the queue appears full even when space is available [1]. A circular queue wraps the rear pointer to reuse these positions [1].

questions.stem: A circular queue of size 5 has front=3, rear=5, size=3. After one DEQUEUE and one ENQUEUE, state the new values of front, rear and size.
questions.ms: DEQUEUE: front=(3 MOD 5)+1=4, size=2 [1]. ENQUEUE: rear=(5 MOD 5)+1=1, size=3 [1]. Final: front=4, rear=1, size=3 [1].

ch13-3.title: 14.3 Linked Lists
ch13-3.subtitle: Nodes, pointers, and insert/delete/traverse operations

keyTerms.name: Linked list
keyTerms.def: A dynamic data structure of nodes, each containing a data item and a pointer to the next node.

keyTerms.name: Node
keyTerms.def: One element of a linked list: stores a data value and a pointer (next node index).

keyTerms.name: Head pointer
keyTerms.def: Points to the first node of the list. NULL/−1 means the list is empty.

keyTerms.name: Null pointer
keyTerms.def: A special pointer value (−1 or NULL) indicating no next node (end of list).

keyTerms.name: Free list
keyTerms.def: A linked list of unused nodes available for new insertions.

ch13-3.theory:
📚 Langfield & Duddell — Ch. 13.10
"In a linear list, items are stored in consecutive locations. In a linked list, each item is stored wherever space is available and linked into an ordered sequence using pointers. An element is called a node. A node has data items and a pointer (variable storing the address of the next node). A pointer that points to nothing is called a null pointer (∅). The address of the first element is stored in a start pointer."

A linked list is usually stored as two parallel arrays: one for data, one for next pointers.

// Example: data=[_, "Ana", "Ben", "Cal"], next=[_, 3, -1, 2], head=1
// head=1 → data[1]="Ana", next[1]=3 → data[3]="Cal", next[3]=2 → data[2]="Ben", next[2]=-1 (end)
// List order: Ana → Cal → Ben

Traversal: Start at head; follow next pointers until −1.

Insert at head: Get a free node, store data, set its next = head, update head.

Delete a node: Find the predecessor, set predecessor.next = node.next, return node to free list.

Advantage over array: insertions and deletions do not require shifting elements. Disadvantage: no random access — must traverse from head.
ch13-3.example:
Insert "Dan" at head (free list head = 4):

1. Take node 4 from free list
2. data[4] ← "Dan"
3. next[4] ← head (= 1)
4. head ← 4
New list: Dan → Ana → Cal → Ben

questions.stem: Describe how you would traverse a linked list to output all items, given the head pointer and next[] array.
questions.ms: Set current ← head [1]; WHILE current ≠ -1 DO OUTPUT data[current]; current ← next[current] ENDWHILE [2].

questions.stem: State one advantage and one disadvantage of a linked list compared to an array for storing a list of items.
questions.ms: Advantage: items can be inserted/deleted without shifting other elements [1]. Disadvantage: no direct (random) access — must traverse from head to reach a specific element [1].

questions.stem: A linked list uses data[] and next[] arrays with head=2. data=[_,"Zoe","Amy","Ben"], next=[_,3,-1,2]. State the order items would be output during traversal.
questions.ms: Start head=2: data[2]="Amy"; next[2]=3: data[3]="Ben"; next[3]=2? — re-check: next=[_, 3, -1, 2] so next[2]= -1 wait. Let me re-read: head=2, data[2]="Amy", next[2]=-1 → output Amy only [1 for Amy]. Actually: head=2: data[2]=Amy, next[2]=-1. Output: Amy [1]. But the question says next=[_,3,-1,2]: index1=3, index2=-1, index3=2. Head=2 → data[2]=Amy, next[2]=-1. Just Amy. Award [2] for correct trace showing Amy only.

ch13-4.title: 14.4 Binary Trees
ch13-4.subtitle: Tree nodes, left/right pointers, and pre/in/post-order traversal

keyTerms.name: Binary tree
keyTerms.def: A tree in which each node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.

keyTerms.name: Root
keyTerms.def: The topmost node of the tree with no parent.

keyTerms.name: Leaf node
keyTerms.def: A node with no children (both left and right pointers are NULL).

keyTerms.name: In-order traversal
keyTerms.def: Visit left subtree, then root, then right subtree. Produces sorted output for a binary search tree.

keyTerms.name: Pre-order traversal
keyTerms.def: Visit root, then left subtree, then right subtree.

keyTerms.name: Post-order traversal
keyTerms.def: Visit left subtree, then right subtree, then root.

ch13-4.theory:
A binary tree is implemented with nodes containing a data value, a left pointer and a right pointer (−1/NULL if no child).

Binary Search Tree (BST) property: every node's left subtree contains only smaller values; right subtree contains only larger values. This allows O(log n) search on average.

Traversal orders (recursive algorithms):

// In-order (Left, Root, Right)
PROCEDURE InOrder(node)
  IF node ≠ NULL THEN
    CALL InOrder(left[node])
    OUTPUT data[node]
    CALL InOrder(right[node])
  ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

Pre-order is used to copy a tree; post-order is used to delete/free a tree.

questions.stem: A binary search tree is built by inserting the values 6, 4, 9, 2, 5 in that order. Draw (describe) the resulting tree and state the in-order traversal output.
questions.ms: Root=6; left=4; 4.left=2; 4.right=5; 6.right=9 [2]. In-order: 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 [1].

questions.stem: State the traversal order that produces a sorted list from a binary search tree and explain why.
questions.ms: In-order (Left, Root, Right) [1]; because the BST property guarantees all left descendants are smaller than the root, which is smaller than all right descendants [1].

questions.stem: State one application of a binary tree in computing.
questions.ms: Any one: storing sorted data for fast search [1]; expression parsing / syntax trees in compilers [1]; Huffman encoding tree [1]; file system directory structure [1].

ch14-1.title: 15.1 File Operations
ch14-1.subtitle: OPENFILE, READFILE, WRITEFILE, CLOSEFILE and file modes

keyTerms.name: OPENFILE
keyTerms.def: Opens a file for reading or writing. Syntax: OPENFILE "filename" FOR READ/WRITE/APPEND

keyTerms.name: READFILE
keyTerms.def: Reads the next line from an open file into a variable.

keyTerms.name: WRITEFILE
keyTerms.def: Writes a value to an open file.

keyTerms.name: CLOSEFILE
keyTerms.def: Closes an open file, flushing any buffered data.

keyTerms.name: READ mode
keyTerms.def: Opens an existing file for reading only.

keyTerms.name: WRITE mode
keyTerms.def: Creates a new file (or overwrites existing) for writing.

keyTerms.name: APPEND mode
keyTerms.def: Opens an existing file and adds new data at the end.

ch14-1.theory:
📚 Langfield & Duddell — Ch. 26.02
"A text file is a sequence of characters stored on a backing store. Each record is stored as a line in the file. The end of a record is marked by a special end-of-line character. The end of the file is marked by the end-of-file marker. The file must be opened before it can be used, and closed when access is complete."

Cambridge 9618 pseudocode uses four file operations. Every file must be opened before use and closed after:

// Writing to a file
OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR WRITE
WRITEFILE "scores.txt", 95
WRITEFILE "scores.txt", 78
CLOSEFILE "scores.txt"

// Reading from a file
DECLARE score : INTEGER
OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "scores.txt", score
OUTPUT score   // 95
CLOSEFILE "scores.txt"

APPEND mode is used to add records without erasing existing data. Always close files — an unclosed file may not be fully written (buffering issue) and can lock the file from other processes.
ch14-1.example:
Log user login with APPEND:

DECLARE username : STRING
username ← "alice"
OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", username & " logged in"
CLOSEFILE "log.txt"

questions.stem: Write pseudocode to open a file called "results.txt", write the values 42 and 87 to it, then close it.
questions.ms: OPENFILE "results.txt" FOR WRITE [1]; WRITEFILE "results.txt", 42; WRITEFILE "results.txt", 87 [1]; CLOSEFILE "results.txt" [1].

questions.stem: State the difference between opening a file in WRITE mode and APPEND mode.
questions.ms: WRITE mode creates a new file or overwrites the existing file from the beginning [1]. APPEND mode opens an existing file and adds new data after the existing content [1].

questions.stem: Explain why it is important to close a file after finishing with it.
questions.ms: Data may be held in a buffer and not written to the file until it is closed [1]; also the file may remain locked, preventing other programs from accessing it [1].

ch14-2.title: 15.2 Sequential File Access
ch14-2.subtitle: Reading sequential files with EOF detection

keyTerms.name: Sequential access
keyTerms.def: Records are read/written in order from the beginning to the end of the file.

keyTerms.name: EOF (End Of File)
keyTerms.def: A marker at the end of a file. Pseudocode function: EOF("filename") returns TRUE when there are no more records.

keyTerms.name: Text file
keyTerms.def: A file where data is stored as human-readable text, one field per line.

ch14-2.theory:
Sequential files are read from beginning to end. Use a WHILE NOT EOF loop to process all records:

DECLARE name  : STRING
DECLARE score : INTEGER
OPENFILE "students.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("students.txt") DO
  READFILE "students.txt", name
  READFILE "students.txt", score
  OUTPUT name & ": " & score
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "students.txt"

Important rules:

  • Each READFILE call reads the next line
  • Check EOF before reading (WHILE NOT EOF) to avoid reading past the end
  • Sequential files cannot be updated in place — you must copy records to a new file
ch14-2.example:
Count records in a file:

DECLARE line  : STRING
DECLARE count : INTEGER
count ← 0
OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("data.txt") DO
  READFILE "data.txt", line
  count ← count + 1
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"
OUTPUT "Records: " & count

questions.stem: Write pseudocode to read all names from a sequential file "names.txt" and output each one, stopping at EOF.
questions.ms: DECLARE name : STRING [1]; OPENFILE "names.txt" FOR READ [1]; WHILE NOT EOF("names.txt") DO READFILE "names.txt", name; OUTPUT name ENDWHILE [1]; CLOSEFILE "names.txt" [1].

questions.stem: Explain why records in a sequential file cannot be updated (changed) in place.
questions.ms: Records are stored as variable-length text; replacing a record with a different-length value would overwrite the start of the next record [1]. The whole file must be rewritten to a new file with the updated record [1].

questions.stem: State the purpose of the EOF() function and what value it returns when all records have been read.
questions.ms: EOF() detects when there are no more records to read in a file [1]; it returns TRUE when the end of the file has been reached [1].

ch14-3.title: 15.3 Random Access Files
ch14-3.subtitle: Direct access using record position and SEEK

keyTerms.name: Random access file
keyTerms.def: A file where any record can be read or written directly by specifying its record number, without reading preceding records.

keyTerms.name: SEEK
keyTerms.def: Moves the file pointer to a specific record position. SEEK("file", n) positions to record n.

keyTerms.name: Fixed-length records
keyTerms.def: Each record occupies the same number of bytes, enabling direct calculation of a record's position.

keyTerms.name: Record number
keyTerms.def: The position of a record within the file (usually 1-based).

ch14-3.theory:
In a random access file, all records are the same size. This means record n starts at byte offset (n−1) × recordSize, enabling direct calculation and instant access without reading other records.

// Read record 3 directly
OPENFILE "stock.dat" FOR RANDOM
SEEK "stock.dat", 3
READFILE "stock.dat", itemRecord
CLOSEFILE "stock.dat"

// Update record 3
OPENFILE "stock.dat" FOR RANDOM
SEEK "stock.dat", 3
WRITEFILE "stock.dat", updatedRecord
CLOSEFILE "stock.dat"

Advantage over sequential: O(1) access to any record — no traversal needed. Ideal for databases, student records, stock files. Disadvantage: requires fixed-length records, which wastes space if records vary in size.
ch14-3.example: A school keeps student records in a random access file, with each student stored at position equal to their ID number. To retrieve student 250: SEEK to position 250 — instant access, regardless of file size.

questions.stem: Explain why random access files require fixed-length records.
questions.ms: Fixed-length records allow the exact byte offset of any record to be calculated from the record number [1]: position = (n−1) × recordSize; variable-length records would make it impossible to calculate the offset without reading all preceding records [1].

questions.stem: State two advantages of random access over sequential access for a large stock-control file.
questions.ms: Any two: a specific record can be accessed directly without reading others [1]; updating a single record does not require rewriting the whole file [1]; faster access time for individual records [1].

questions.stem: Write pseudocode to open a random access file "library.dat", seek to record 7, read it into variable bookRec, then close the file.
questions.ms: OPENFILE "library.dat" FOR RANDOM [1]; SEEK "library.dat", 7 [1]; READFILE "library.dat", bookRec; CLOSEFILE "library.dat" [1].

ch15-1.title: 15.1 Classes & Objects
ch15-1.subtitle: Class definition, attributes, methods and instantiation

keyTerms.name: Class
keyTerms.def: A blueprint/template that defines the attributes (data) and methods (behaviour) of a type of object.

keyTerms.name: Object
keyTerms.def: An instance of a class — a specific entity created from the blueprint.

keyTerms.name: Attribute
keyTerms.def: A variable that belongs to an object (its state/properties).

keyTerms.name: Method
keyTerms.def: A procedure or function defined inside a class that operates on an object's attributes.

keyTerms.name: Constructor
keyTerms.def: A special method called when an object is created (often named NEW or the class name).

keyTerms.name: Instantiation
keyTerms.def: The act of creating a specific object from a class using NEW.

ch15-1.theory:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) models the world as interacting objects. A class is the design; an object is a built instance.

Cambridge 9618 pseudocode class syntax:

CLASS Animal
  PRIVATE name   : STRING
  PRIVATE sound  : STRING

  PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(n : STRING, s : STRING)
    name  ← n
    sound ← s
  ENDPROCEDURE

  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Speak()
    OUTPUT name & " says " & sound
  ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

DECLARE cat : Animal
cat ← NEW Animal("Whiskers", "meow")
CALL cat.Speak()   // "Whiskers says meow"
ch15-1.example:
BankAccount class with deposit:

CLASS BankAccount
  PRIVATE balance : REAL
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(initial : REAL)
    balance ← initial
  ENDPROCEDURE
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Deposit(amount : REAL)
    balance ← balance + amount
  ENDPROCEDURE
  PUBLIC FUNCTION GetBalance() RETURNS REAL
    RETURN balance
  ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

questions.stem: State the difference between a class and an object.
questions.ms: A class is a template/blueprint defining attributes and methods [1]; an object is a specific instance created from that class [1].

questions.stem: Write pseudocode for a class Rectangle with PRIVATE attributes width and height (both REAL), a constructor that sets them, and a PUBLIC function Area() that returns width × height.
questions.ms: CLASS Rectangle [1]; PRIVATE width, height : REAL [1]; PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(w, h): width←w; height←h ENDPROCEDURE [1]; PUBLIC FUNCTION Area() RETURNS REAL; RETURN width * height; ENDFUNCTION [1]; ENDCLASS [1].

questions.stem: Explain what a constructor method does and when it is called.
questions.ms: A constructor initialises an object's attributes with starting values [1]; it is called automatically when an object is created with NEW [1].

ch15-2.title: 15.2 Inheritance
ch15-2.subtitle: Superclass, subclass, INHERITS FROM and method overriding

keyTerms.name: Inheritance
keyTerms.def: A mechanism where a subclass acquires (inherits) the attributes and methods of its superclass.

keyTerms.name: Superclass (base class)
keyTerms.def: The class being inherited from; provides common attributes and methods.

keyTerms.name: Subclass (derived class)
keyTerms.def: The class that inherits from the superclass and may add or override features.

keyTerms.name: INHERITS FROM
keyTerms.def: Cambridge pseudocode keyword to declare inheritance: CLASS Dog INHERITS FROM Animal

keyTerms.name: Method overriding
keyTerms.def: Defining a method in a subclass with the same name as in the superclass, replacing the superclass behaviour.

ch15-2.theory:
Inheritance supports code reuse. A subclass inherits all PUBLIC members of its superclass and can add new ones or override existing ones.

CLASS Animal
  PRIVATE name : STRING
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(n : STRING)
    name ← n
  ENDPROCEDURE
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Speak()
    OUTPUT "..."
  ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

CLASS Dog INHERITS FROM Animal
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Speak()   // override
    OUTPUT "Woof!"
  ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

DECLARE d : Dog
d ← NEW Dog("Rex")
CALL d.Speak()   // "Woof!" — overridden method

The subclass Dog inherits name and the constructor from Animal, but replaces Speak().
ch15-2.example:
Shape → Circle hierarchy:

CLASS Shape
  PUBLIC FUNCTION Area() RETURNS REAL
    RETURN 0
  ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

CLASS Circle INHERITS FROM Shape
  PRIVATE radius : REAL
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(r : REAL)
    radius ← r
  ENDPROCEDURE
  PUBLIC FUNCTION Area() RETURNS REAL
    RETURN 3.14159 * radius * radius
  ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

questions.stem: Class Vehicle has attributes speed and colour. Class Car inherits from Vehicle and adds attribute numDoors. Write the pseudocode class header for Car using Cambridge syntax.
questions.ms: CLASS Car INHERITS FROM Vehicle [1]; with PRIVATE numDoors : INTEGER (or similar attribute) [1].

questions.stem: Explain what "method overriding" means and give a reason why it is useful.
questions.ms: Overriding is defining a method in a subclass with the same name as a superclass method, replacing its behaviour [1]. It allows subclasses to provide specialised implementations while sharing a common interface [1].

questions.stem: State two benefits of using inheritance in a large program.
questions.ms: Any two: reduces code duplication — shared code written once in superclass [1]; changes to shared behaviour only need to be made in one place [1]; easier to extend the program by adding new subclasses [1].

ch15-3.title: 15.3 Polymorphism
ch15-3.subtitle: Same method name, different behaviour across related classes

keyTerms.name: Polymorphism
keyTerms.def: The ability to call the same method on different objects and get different results depending on the object's class.

keyTerms.name: Method overriding
keyTerms.def: The mechanism that enables polymorphism — each subclass provides its own version of an inherited method.

keyTerms.name: Dynamic dispatch
keyTerms.def: The runtime mechanism that determines which overridden method to call based on the actual object type.

ch15-3.theory:
Polymorphism (Greek: "many forms") means one interface, many implementations. When different classes share a common method name but each implements it differently, code that works on the superclass type automatically calls the correct version for each object.

// Each subclass overrides Speak()
CLASS Cat INHERITS FROM Animal
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Speak()
    OUTPUT "Meow"
  ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

CLASS Cow INHERITS FROM Animal
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Speak()
    OUTPUT "Moo"
  ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

// Polymorphic call — same method, different result
DECLARE animals : ARRAY[1:2] OF Animal
animals[1] ← NEW Cat()
animals[2] ← NEW Cow()
FOR i ← 1 TO 2
  CALL animals[i].Speak()   // "Meow" then "Moo"
NEXT i
ch15-3.example: Shape area polymorphism: A Shape array holds Circle and Rectangle objects. Calling Area() on each element automatically calls the correct formula without needing to know which shape it is.

questions.stem: Define polymorphism and explain how it relates to method overriding.
questions.ms: Polymorphism is the ability to call the same method on objects of different classes and get a class-appropriate result [1]. It is achieved through method overriding [1] — each subclass provides its own implementation of the inherited method [1].

questions.stem: State one benefit of polymorphism to a programmer writing a system that handles multiple shapes.
questions.ms: The programmer can write generic code (e.g. a loop calling Area()) that works correctly for any shape without needing separate IF/CASE branches for each shape type [1].

questions.stem: Class Employee has a method CalculatePay(). Classes FullTime and PartTime both inherit from Employee and override this method. Explain why this is an example of polymorphism.
questions.ms: Both subclasses use the same method name CalculatePay() [1] but each computes pay differently — the correct version is called based on the actual object type at runtime [1].

ch15-4.title: 15.4 Encapsulation & Paradigms
ch15-4.subtitle: Private/public access, getters/setters and programming paradigms

keyTerms.name: Encapsulation
keyTerms.def: Bundling data (attributes) and methods together in a class, and restricting direct access to attributes by making them PRIVATE.

keyTerms.name: Information hiding
keyTerms.def: Preventing external code from directly reading or modifying an object's attributes (enforced by PRIVATE).

keyTerms.name: Getter (accessor)
keyTerms.def: A PUBLIC function that returns the value of a PRIVATE attribute.

keyTerms.name: Setter (mutator)
keyTerms.def: A PUBLIC procedure that validates and sets the value of a PRIVATE attribute.

keyTerms.name: Declarative paradigm
keyTerms.def: Programs describe what result is wanted, not how to compute it (e.g. SQL, Prolog).

keyTerms.name: Procedural paradigm
keyTerms.def: Programs are a sequence of statements that describe step-by-step how to solve a problem.

ch15-4.theory:
Encapsulation protects an object's internal state. Attributes are declared PRIVATE; only the object's own methods can access them directly. External code uses PUBLIC getters and setters:

CLASS Student
  PRIVATE mark : INTEGER

  PUBLIC PROCEDURE SetMark(m : INTEGER)
    IF m >= 0 AND m <= 100
      THEN mark ← m
      ELSE OUTPUT "Invalid mark"
    ENDIF
  ENDPROCEDURE

  PUBLIC FUNCTION GetMark() RETURNS INTEGER
    RETURN mark
  ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

The setter validates input — direct attribute access would bypass this check.

Programming paradigms: Procedural (step-by-step, Cambridge pseudocode), Object-oriented (classes and objects), Declarative (state the goal — SQL SELECT, Prolog facts and rules).
ch15-4.example: SQL is declarative: SELECT name FROM students WHERE mark > 70 — you state what you want; the database engine decides how to retrieve it. No loops or conditionals needed.

questions.stem: Explain what encapsulation means in OOP and state one benefit of making attributes PRIVATE.
questions.ms: Encapsulation bundles data and methods in a class and restricts direct access to attributes using PRIVATE [1]. Benefit: prevents external code from setting attributes to invalid values; data can only be changed through validated setter methods [1].

questions.stem: Write a PUBLIC getter method GetAge() for a class that has a PRIVATE INTEGER attribute age.
questions.ms: PUBLIC FUNCTION GetAge() RETURNS INTEGER [1]; RETURN age; ENDFUNCTION [1].

questions.stem: State one difference between procedural programming and declarative programming. Give an example of a language for each.
questions.ms: Procedural describes how to solve the problem step by step [1] — e.g. Pascal/Python. Declarative describes what result is required [1] — e.g. SQL/Prolog.

ch16-1.title: 16.1 Big-O Notation
ch16-1.subtitle: Measuring algorithm efficiency — time and space complexity

keyTerms.name: Big-O
keyTerms.def: Upper bound on growth rate of algorithm run time as input size n increases.

keyTerms.name: O(1)
keyTerms.def: Constant time — execution time does not grow with input size.

keyTerms.name: O(n)
keyTerms.def: Linear time — execution grows proportionally with input size.

keyTerms.name: O(n²)
keyTerms.def: Quadratic time — common in nested loops over the same data.

keyTerms.name: O(log n)
keyTerms.def: Logarithmic time — input halved each step; e.g. binary search.

ch16-1.theory:
Big-O notation describes the worst-case growth rate of an algorithm. Common complexities (best → worst):
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)

When simplifying: drop constants and lower-order terms. O(3n² + 2n + 7) → O(n²).
ch16-1.example:
Nested loop → O(n²):

FOR i ← 1 TO n
  FOR j ← 1 TO n
    OUTPUT i * j
  NEXT j
NEXT i

Outer loop × inner loop = n × n = n² operations.

questions.stem: State the Big-O complexity of a single FOR loop from 1 to n with constant-time operations inside.
An algorithm has complexity O(n²). State what happens to execution time when n doubles.
questions.ms: Time increases by a factor of 4 (2²=4) [2].

questions.stem: Compare O(n) and O(log n) complexity and explain why binary search is more efficient for large n.
questions.ms: O(n) grows linearly [1]; O(log n) grows logarithmically [1]; binary search halves the search space each step [1]; for large n, log n grows far more slowly than n [1].

ch16-2.title: 16.2 Dijkstra's Algorithm
ch16-2.subtitle: Finding shortest paths in weighted graphs

keyTerms.name: Weighted graph
keyTerms.def: Graph where edges have numerical weights representing cost or distance.

keyTerms.name: Dijkstra's
keyTerms.def: Greedy algorithm finding shortest path from source to all vertices.

keyTerms.name: Priority queue
keyTerms.def: Data structure returning the element with lowest priority value first.

ch16-2.theory:
Steps:

  1. Set dist[source]=0, dist[all others]=∞
  2. Add all vertices to unvisited set
  3. While unvisited not empty: pick vertex u with minimum dist
  4. For each neighbour v: if dist[u]+weight(u,v) < dist[v], update dist[v]
  5. Mark u visited

Complexity: O(V²) with matrix; O((V+E)log V) with priority queue.
ch16-2.example:
Graph A→C(1), C→B(2), A→B(4), B→D(1), C→D(5).
From A: visit A(0)→update C=1, B=4. Visit C(1)→update B=3, D=6. Visit B(3)→update D=4. Shortest A→D = 4.

questions.stem: State two conditions required for Dijkstra's algorithm to guarantee the shortest path.
questions.ms: Non-negative edge weights [1]; graph must be connected / all vertices reachable [1].

questions.stem: Describe the role of the 'unvisited set' in Dijkstra's algorithm.
questions.ms: Tracks vertices not yet permanently assigned shortest distance [1]; ensures each vertex processed exactly once [1].

ch16-3.title: 16.3 A* Search
ch16-3.subtitle: Heuristic-guided optimal pathfinding

keyTerms.name: Heuristic h(n)
keyTerms.def: Estimate of cost from node n to goal — guides search direction.

keyTerms.name: f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
keyTerms.def: Total estimated cost: actual cost so far plus heuristic estimate.

keyTerms.name: Admissible heuristic
keyTerms.def: Never overestimates true cost — guarantees optimality.

ch16-3.theory:
A* extends Dijkstra's by adding a heuristic h(n) to focus search towards the goal. At each step, expand the node with lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n).

If h(n) is admissible, A* guarantees the optimal path and explores fewer nodes than Dijkstra's.
ch16-3.example: Grid pathfinding: straight-line distance to goal is admissible. A* prioritises cells closer to the goal rather than exploring all directions equally like Dijkstra's.

questions.stem: Explain why an admissible heuristic is necessary for A* to guarantee an optimal solution.
questions.ms: Overestimating h(n) may cause A* to bypass the optimal path [1]; admissible means h(n) ≤ true remaining cost [1]; ensures no cheaper path is wrongly dismissed [1].

ch16-4.title: 16.4 Dynamic Programming
ch16-4.subtitle: Solving overlapping subproblems efficiently

keyTerms.name: Memoisation
keyTerms.def: Cache results of subproblems to avoid recomputation (top-down).

keyTerms.name: Tabulation
keyTerms.def: Fill a table iteratively from base cases (bottom-up).

keyTerms.name: Optimal substructure
keyTerms.def: Optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems.

ch16-4.theory:
DP applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Instead of recomputing, store results → drastic speedup.

Fibonacci naively: O(2ⁿ). With memoisation: O(n).
ch16-4.example:
DECLARE memo : ARRAY[0:50] OF INTEGER
FUNCTION Fib(n)
  IF n <= 1 THEN RETURN n ENDIF
  IF memo[n] <> -1 THEN RETURN memo[n] ENDIF
  memo[n] ← Fib(n-1) + Fib(n-2)
  RETURN memo[n]
ENDFUNCTION

questions.stem: State two conditions a problem must satisfy for dynamic programming to be applicable.
questions.ms: Optimal substructure [1]; overlapping subproblems [1].

questions.stem: Compare memoisation and tabulation as DP approaches.
questions.ms: Memoisation: top-down recursive, only computes needed subproblems [2]. Tabulation: bottom-up iterative, computes all subproblems but avoids recursion overhead [2].

ch16-5.title: 16.5 Backtracking
ch16-5.subtitle: Systematic exhaustive search with constraint pruning

keyTerms.name: Backtracking
keyTerms.def: Build solutions incrementally; abandon paths violating constraints.

keyTerms.name: Pruning
keyTerms.def: Eliminating branches that cannot lead to a valid solution.

ch16-5.theory:
Backtracking builds a solution step by step and abandons a partial solution as soon as a constraint is violated, then tries the next alternative.

PROCEDURE Solve(state)
  IF complete(state) THEN output; RETURN ENDIF
  FOR each choice DO
    IF valid(state+choice) THEN
      apply; Solve(state+choice); undo
    ENDIF
  NEXT
ENDPROCEDURE
ch16-5.example: N-Queens: Place N queens so none attack each other. Try each column in each row; if conflict, backtrack to previous row and try next column. Pruning eliminates infeasible branches early.

questions.stem: Explain the purpose of the "undo" step in backtracking.
questions.ms: Restores state before the choice [1]; allows trying a different choice at the same point [1].

ch17-1.title: 17.1 Hash Tables
ch17-1.subtitle: O(1) average lookup using hash functions

keyTerms.name: Hash function
keyTerms.def: Maps a key to an array index.

keyTerms.name: Collision
keyTerms.def: Two keys produce the same index.

keyTerms.name: Chaining
keyTerms.def: Store collisions in a linked list at each bucket.

keyTerms.name: Open addressing
keyTerms.def: Probe for the next empty slot on collision.

keyTerms.name: Load factor
keyTerms.def: Ratio of entries to table capacity; high load → more collisions.

ch17-1.theory:
Hash tables provide average O(1) insert, delete, and lookup. Hash function: index = key MOD tableSize (use prime size to reduce clustering).

Collision resolution: Chaining (linked list per bucket) or Open addressing (linear/quadratic probing).
ch17-1.example: Size=7. Keys 10,22,31: hash(k)=k MOD 7 → 3,1,3. Collision at 3! With chaining: slot 3 holds [10,31]. Lookup O(1) average, O(n) worst case.

questions.stem: Explain why a prime number is often chosen as hash table size.
questions.ms: Reduces clustering [1]; prime has no common factors with typical key values, producing more uniform distribution [1].

questions.stem: Compare chaining and open addressing for collision resolution.
questions.ms: Chaining: linked list per slot, handles arbitrary collisions, extra memory for pointers [2]. Open addressing: probes within array, better cache performance, degrades at high load factor [2].

ch17-2.title: 17.2 Heaps and Priority Queues
ch17-2.subtitle: Efficient min/max retrieval using a complete binary tree

keyTerms.name: Max-heap
keyTerms.def: Each parent ≥ its children.

keyTerms.name: Min-heap
keyTerms.def: Each parent ≤ its children.

keyTerms.name: Sift-up
keyTerms.def: Restore heap after insertion by swapping with parent.

keyTerms.name: Sift-down
keyTerms.def: Restore heap after removal by swapping root with largest child.

ch17-2.theory:
Binary heap stored as 1-based array: parent(i) = i DIV 2; left child = 2i; right = 2i+1.

Insert: append, sift-up → O(log n). Extract max/min: swap root with last, remove, sift-down → O(log n).

Used in Dijkstra's priority queue and heap sort.
ch17-2.example: Max-heap [90,80,70,50,60]. Insert 85: append → [90,80,70,50,60,85]. Parent of 6 is 3 (value 70). 85>70 → swap. Parent of 3 is 1 (value 90). 85<90 → stop. Result: [90,80,85,50,60,70].

questions.stem: Describe the steps to insert a new element into a min-heap.
questions.ms: Append element at end of array [1]; compare with parent: if smaller, swap [1]; repeat until heap property satisfied or root reached (sift-up) [1].

ch17-3.title: 17.3 Graph Representation
ch17-3.subtitle: Adjacency matrix vs adjacency list

keyTerms.name: Adjacency matrix
keyTerms.def: n×n grid; cell [i,j] = weight if edge exists.

keyTerms.name: Adjacency list
keyTerms.def: Array of lists; each list holds neighbours of that vertex.

keyTerms.name: Directed graph
keyTerms.def: Edges have direction.

keyTerms.name: Weighted graph
keyTerms.def: Edges carry numerical values.

ch17-3.theory:
Matrix: O(1) edge lookup; O(V²) space — good for dense graphs.

List: O(V+E) space — efficient for sparse graphs; iteration over neighbours faster.
ch17-3.example:
Graph A-B(3), A-C(1), B-D(5).
Matrix (3×3): [0,3,1; 3,0,0; 1,0,0]. D added: 4×4 matrix.
List: A:[B(3),C(1)], B:[A(3),D(5)], C:[A(1)], D:[B(5)].

questions.stem: State one advantage of adjacency list over adjacency matrix.
questions.ms: Uses O(V+E) space instead of O(V²) — more efficient for sparse graphs [1].

questions.stem: Explain when an adjacency matrix would be preferred over an adjacency list.
questions.ms: When the graph is dense (many edges) [1]; when O(1) edge existence lookups are needed frequently [1].

ch17-4.title: 17.4 Graph Traversals (BFS/DFS)
ch17-4.subtitle: Systematically visiting every vertex

keyTerms.name: BFS
keyTerms.def: Breadth-First Search — level by level using a queue.

keyTerms.name: DFS
keyTerms.def: Depth-First Search — deep first using a stack or recursion.

ch17-4.theory:
BFS: Enqueue start; while not empty: dequeue u, visit unvisited neighbours and enqueue them. Finds shortest unweighted path. O(V+E).

DFS: Push start; while not empty: pop u, if unvisited: mark and push neighbours. O(V+E). Used for cycle detection, topological sort.
ch17-4.example:
Graph A-B,A-C,B-D,C-D,D-E from A:
BFS: A→B,C→D→E (levels).
DFS: A→B→D→E→C (depth first).

questions.stem: Explain why BFS is preferred for finding the shortest unweighted path.
questions.ms: BFS explores vertices in order of distance from source [1]; first time destination reached is the shortest path [1]; DFS may find longer path first [1].

ch18-1.title: 18.1 Relational Model and SQL
ch18-1.subtitle: Tables, keys, and structured queries

keyTerms.name: Primary key
keyTerms.def: Attribute(s) uniquely identifying each row in a table.

keyTerms.name: Foreign key
keyTerms.def: Attribute referencing primary key of another table — enforces referential integrity.

keyTerms.name: JOIN
keyTerms.def: Combines rows from two tables on a matching column.

keyTerms.name: Aggregate functions
keyTerms.def: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN — operate on groups of rows.

ch18-1.theory:
The relational model stores data in tables (relations). SQL is the standard language for querying.

SELECT col1, col2
FROM table1
JOIN table2 ON table1.id = table2.id
WHERE condition
GROUP BY col
HAVING agg_condition
ORDER BY col ASC
ch18-1.example:
Tables: Student(StudentID, Name, CourseID), Course(CourseID, Title)

SELECT Student.Name, Course.Title
FROM Student
JOIN Course ON Student.CourseID = Course.CourseID
WHERE Course.Title = 'Computer Science'
ORDER BY Student.Name ASC

questions.stem: Write SQL to find the average mark and number of students for subject Computer Science from table Marks(StudentID, Subject, Mark).
questions.ms: SELECT AVG(Mark), COUNT(StudentID) [1] FROM Marks [1] WHERE Subject = 'Computer Science' [2].

ch18-2.title: 18.2 Normalisation (1NF–3NF)
ch18-2.subtitle: Eliminating redundancy and update anomalies

keyTerms.name: 1NF
keyTerms.def: Atomic values; no repeating groups; primary key defined.

keyTerms.name: 2NF
keyTerms.def: 1NF + no partial dependency on composite key.

keyTerms.name: 3NF
keyTerms.def: 2NF + no transitive dependency between non-key attributes.

ch18-2.theory:
1NF: Each cell atomic, no repeating groups.
2NF: All non-key attributes depend on the whole composite key.
3NF: Non-key attributes depend only on the primary key, not on each other (no transitive dependency).
ch18-2.example:
3NF violation: Order(OrderID, CustomerID, CustomerCity). CustomerCity depends on CustomerID, not OrderID → transitive dependency.
Fix: Order(OrderID, CustomerID) + Customer(CustomerID, CustomerCity).

questions.stem: Table: Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID, CourseName, Grade). Which normal form is violated? Explain.
questions.ms: Violates 2NF [1]; CourseName depends on CourseID alone [1], not the full composite key (StudentID, CourseID) [1]; this is a partial dependency [1].

ch18-3.title: 18.3 ACID and Transactions
ch18-3.subtitle: Guaranteeing reliability in concurrent databases

keyTerms.name: Atomicity
keyTerms.def: All operations succeed or all roll back.

keyTerms.name: Consistency
