keyTerms.def: Transaction moves DB from one valid state to another.

keyTerms.name: Isolation
keyTerms.def: Concurrent transactions do not interfere.

keyTerms.name: Durability
keyTerms.def: Committed changes persist after failure.

ch18-3.theory:
ACID ensures reliable transactions. Atomicity prevents partial updates. Isolation uses record locking. Durability uses write-ahead logs.

Deadlock in DB: T1 locks Row A, waits for Row B. T2 locks Row B, waits for Row A → resolved by timeout or lock ordering.
ch18-3.example:
BEGIN TRANSACTION
  UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'A'
  UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 'B'
COMMIT

If crash between statements: atomicity rolls back the debit.

questions.stem: Explain how atomicity prevents data corruption in a bank transfer.
questions.ms: Transaction treated as indivisible unit [1]; if any operation fails all changes rolled back [1]; prevents money being debited but not credited [1].

ch18-4.title: 18.4 Entity-Relationship Diagrams
ch18-4.subtitle: Modelling entities, attributes, and relationships

keyTerms.name: Entity
keyTerms.def: Real-world object represented as a table.

keyTerms.name: One-to-many (1:N)
keyTerms.def: One entity relates to many instances of another.

keyTerms.name: Many-to-many (M:N)
keyTerms.def: Resolved by a junction/linking table.

ch18-4.theory: ER diagrams show entities and relationships with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N). M:N relationships require a junction table with foreign keys from both sides.
ch18-4.example:
Student ─── enrolls in ──< Course (M:N).
Resolved: Enrolment(StudentID [FK], CourseID [FK], Grade).

questions.stem: Explain why M:N relationships cannot be directly implemented and how to resolve them.
questions.ms: Cannot store multiple FK values in one field — violates 1NF [1]; M:N requires a junction table [1]; junction holds FK from both entities [1]; composite PK of the junction ensures uniqueness [1].

ch19-1.title: 19.1 Process Scheduling
ch19-1.subtitle: OS algorithms for sharing CPU time

keyTerms.name: Round-robin
keyTerms.def: Each process gets equal CPU time slices in rotation.

keyTerms.name: SJF
keyTerms.def: Shortest Job First — minimum average wait, but can starve long jobs.

keyTerms.name: FCFS
keyTerms.def: First-Come First-Served — simple but poor for short jobs behind long ones.

keyTerms.name: Starvation
keyTerms.def: Low-priority processes never get CPU time.

ch19-1.theory:
Round-robin: Each process runs for one quantum (e.g. 20ms) before context switch. Fair; good for interactive systems.
SJF: Optimal average wait but requires knowing burst length; starves long processes.
FCFS: Simple; convoy effect — short jobs wait behind long ones.
ch19-1.example:
P1(10ms), P2(4ms), P3(2ms) at t=0.
FCFS avg wait: (0+10+14)/3 = 8ms
SJF avg wait: P3→P2→P1: (0+2+6)/3 = 2.67ms

questions.stem: Compare round-robin and SJF scheduling for fairness and average wait time.
questions.ms: Round-robin: fair, all get equal time [1]; average wait can be high for short jobs behind long ones [1]. SJF: minimises average wait [1]; unfair — long processes may starve [1].

ch19-2.title: 19.2 Deadlock
ch19-2.subtitle: Circular resource waiting and prevention strategies

keyTerms.name: Deadlock
keyTerms.def: Processes each wait for resources held by others — none can proceed.

keyTerms.name: Coffman conditions
keyTerms.def: Four necessary conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.

keyTerms.name: Banker's algorithm
keyTerms.def: Deadlock avoidance: only grant request if safe state maintained.

ch19-2.theory: Deadlock requires ALL four Coffman conditions simultaneously. Prevention: eliminate one condition (e.g. require all locks acquired at once eliminates hold-and-wait). Avoidance: Banker's algorithm. Detection + Recovery: find cycle in resource graph; kill/rollback a process.
ch19-2.example:
P1 holds Lock A, waits for Lock B. P2 holds Lock B, waits for Lock A → deadlock.
Prevention: require alphabetical lock ordering → P2 must acquire A before B → no circular wait.

questions.stem: State the four Coffman conditions and explain how eliminating one prevents deadlock.
questions.ms: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait [2]. Eliminating any one breaks the deadlock cycle; e.g. disallowing hold-and-wait means process requests all resources at once [2].

ch19-3.title: 19.3 Virtual Memory and Paging
ch19-3.subtitle: Extending RAM using disk-based page swapping

keyTerms.name: Virtual memory
keyTerms.def: Disk space used as extension of RAM.

keyTerms.name: Page
keyTerms.def: Fixed-size block of virtual address space.

keyTerms.name: Frame
keyTerms.def: Fixed-size block of physical RAM.

keyTerms.name: Page fault
keyTerms.def: Accessing a page not currently in RAM.

keyTerms.name: Thrashing
keyTerms.def: System spends more time paging than executing.

ch19-3.theory:
Virtual memory divides address space into pages; RAM into frames. The page table maps virtual pages to physical frames. On a page fault, OS loads the required page from disk (evicting another page using LRU or FIFO).

Thrashing: occurs when working set exceeds available frames — fix by reducing multiprogramming or adding RAM.
ch19-3.example: 3 frames, access sequence 1,2,3,4,1,2,5: with FIFO eviction → 7 page faults. With LRU → fewer faults.

questions.stem: Explain what a page fault is and the steps the OS takes to handle it.
questions.ms: Page fault: process accesses virtual page not in RAM [1]; OS suspends process [1]; loads page from disk into a free/evicted frame [1]; updates page table and resumes process [1].

ch20-1.title: 20.1 Knowledge Representation
ch20-1.subtitle: Encoding expert knowledge for machine reasoning

keyTerms.name: Knowledge base
keyTerms.def: Collection of facts and IF-THEN rules in an expert system.

keyTerms.name: Production rules
keyTerms.def: IF condition THEN action statements encoding expert heuristics.

keyTerms.name: Semantic network
keyTerms.def: Graph of concepts connected by labelled relationship edges.

ch20-1.theory: Expert systems capture specialist knowledge in a knowledge base of facts and rules. An inference engine applies rules to reach conclusions. Limitations: knowledge acquisition bottleneck; cannot learn; struggle with uncertainty.
ch20-1.example:
IF fever = TRUE AND rash = TRUE
   THEN disease = "measles" [confidence 0.8]
IF disease = "measles"
   THEN treatment = "rest and fluids"

questions.stem: Describe two limitations of rule-based expert systems.
questions.ms: Knowledge acquisition is slow and difficult [1]; experts struggle to articulate all knowledge [1]; cannot learn from new cases without manual updates [1]; poor handling of uncertainty [1]. (Any 2 × 2)

ch20-2.title: 20.2 Inference Engines
ch20-2.subtitle: Forward chaining and backward chaining

keyTerms.name: Forward chaining
keyTerms.def: Data-driven: start from facts, apply rules, derive conclusions.

keyTerms.name: Backward chaining
keyTerms.def: Goal-driven: start from goal, find supporting facts by working backwards.

ch20-2.theory:
Forward: Apply all matching rules to current facts, add new facts, repeat. Used when all data available — monitoring/alerting systems.

Backward: Set a goal; find rules whose conclusion matches; make conditions sub-goals; recurse. Used for diagnosis — confirming a specific hypothesis.
ch20-2.example:
Rules: fever→ill, ill+cough→flu. Facts: {fever, cough}.
Forward: fever→ill, ill+cough→flu. Backward (goal=flu): need ill+cough → need fever → check: ✓ all found.

questions.stem: Compare forward and backward chaining with a suitable scenario for each.
questions.ms: Forward: data-driven, derives conclusions from known facts [1]; good for monitoring where all inputs known [1]. Backward: goal-driven, finds supporting facts [1]; good for diagnosis to confirm/refute specific hypothesis [1].

ch20-3.title: 20.3 Machine Learning Concepts
ch20-3.subtitle: Systems that learn patterns from data

keyTerms.name: Supervised learning
keyTerms.def: Model trained on labelled input-output pairs.

keyTerms.name: Unsupervised learning
keyTerms.def: Model finds patterns in unlabelled data.

keyTerms.name: Neural network
keyTerms.def: Layered connected nodes; weights adjusted during training.

keyTerms.name: Overfitting
keyTerms.def: Model fits training data too closely; fails to generalise.

ch20-3.theory:
Types: Supervised (classification, regression), Unsupervised (clustering), Reinforcement (reward/penalty).

Neural networks: Input → Hidden layers → Output. Trained via backpropagation adjusting weights to minimise error.

Overfitting prevention: validation set, regularisation, simpler model, more data.
ch20-3.example: Spam filter trained on 10,000 emails: 95% training accuracy but 80% on new emails → overfitting. Solution: increase training data size, use cross-validation.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning with an example of each.
questions.ms: Supervised: trained on labelled data [1]; example: image classification with cat/dog labels [1]. Unsupervised: finds patterns in unlabelled data [1]; example: customer clustering by purchase behaviour [1].

ch21-1.title: 21.1 Design Patterns
ch21-1.subtitle: Reusable solutions to common software design problems

keyTerms.name: Design pattern
keyTerms.def: A reusable solution template for a recurring software design problem.

keyTerms.name: Singleton
keyTerms.def: Ensures a class has only one instance with a global access point.

keyTerms.name: Strategy
keyTerms.def: Defines a family of algorithms; encapsulates and makes them interchangeable.

keyTerms.name: Observer
keyTerms.def: Defines one-to-many dependency; when one object changes, its dependents are notified.

keyTerms.name: Factory Method
keyTerms.def: Defines an interface for creating objects; subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

ch21-1.theory:
Creational patterns (Singleton, Factory) control object creation. Structural patterns (Adapter, Decorator) manage class composition. Behavioural patterns (Strategy, Observer) handle object communication.

Singleton: Constructor private; static method returns the one shared instance. Thread-safety consideration in multi-threaded environments.

Strategy: Context holds a reference to a Strategy interface. Clients set the strategy at runtime — eliminates conditional logic.

Observer: Subject maintains a list of observers; calls notify() on state change. Decouples subject from its observers.
ch21-1.example:
Singleton in pseudocode:

CLASS Logger
  PRIVATE STATIC instance : Logger
  PRIVATE PROCEDURE NEW()
  ENDPROCEDURE
  PUBLIC STATIC FUNCTION GetInstance() RETURNS Logger
    IF instance = NULL THEN
      instance ← NEW Logger()
    ENDIF
    RETURN instance
  ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

questions.stem: Describe the Singleton pattern and give one scenario where it would be appropriate.
questions.ms: Restricts a class to a single instance [1]; uses a private constructor and static accessor method [1]; appropriate for: database connection manager / configuration settings / logging service [1].

questions.stem: Explain the advantage of the Strategy pattern over using an IF/CASE statement to select algorithms.
questions.ms: Open/closed principle — new algorithms added without modifying existing code [1]; strategies can be swapped at runtime without changing the context class [1].

ch21-2.title: 21.2 Abstract Classes and Interfaces
ch21-2.subtitle: Defining contracts and enforcing structure

keyTerms.name: Abstract class
keyTerms.def: A class that cannot be instantiated; may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement.

keyTerms.name: Abstract method
keyTerms.def: A method declared without implementation; all non-abstract subclasses must override it.

keyTerms.name: Interface
keyTerms.def: A completely abstract type specifying method signatures — a pure contract with no implementation.

keyTerms.name: Concrete class
keyTerms.def: A class that provides implementations for all methods and can be instantiated.

ch21-2.theory:
Abstract classes use the keyword ABSTRACT. They can have both abstract and concrete methods. A class inheriting an abstract class must implement all abstract methods or itself be abstract.

Interfaces define only method signatures (no implementation). A class can implement multiple interfaces but inherit only one class (in most languages).

When to use which: Abstract class — shared implementation + contract. Interface — pure contract with no shared code (unrelated classes sharing behaviour).
ch21-2.example:
ABSTRACT CLASS Shape
  PUBLIC ABSTRACT FUNCTION Area() RETURNS REAL
  PUBLIC FUNCTION Describe() RETURNS STRING
    RETURN "I am a shape with area: " & Area()
  ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

CLASS Circle INHERITS Shape
  PRIVATE r : REAL
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(radius : REAL)
    r ← radius
  ENDPROCEDURE
  PUBLIC FUNCTION Area() RETURNS REAL
    RETURN 3.14159 * r * r
  ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

questions.stem: State two differences between an abstract class and an interface.
questions.ms: Abstract class can have concrete (implemented) methods / interfaces cannot [1]; a class can implement multiple interfaces but only inherit one abstract class [1].

questions.stem: A program uses Shape, Circle, Rectangle and Triangle. Explain why Shape should be abstract.
questions.ms: A Shape object on its own has no meaningful area/perimeter [1]; forces all subclasses to provide their own Area() implementation [1].

ch21-3.title: 21.3 Polymorphism in Depth
ch21-3.subtitle: Runtime and compile-time polymorphism

keyTerms.name: Polymorphism
keyTerms.def: The ability of objects of different types to be treated as instances of a common supertype.

keyTerms.name: Method overriding
keyTerms.def: Subclass provides a different implementation of a method defined in its superclass.

keyTerms.name: Method overloading
keyTerms.def: Multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class.

keyTerms.name: Dynamic dispatch
keyTerms.def: The process of selecting which overridden method to call at runtime based on the actual object type.

keyTerms.name: Late binding
keyTerms.def: Method calls resolved at runtime rather than compile time.

ch21-3.theory:
Runtime polymorphism (method overriding + dynamic dispatch): the correct method is selected based on the actual object type, not the reference type. Enables writing code against the supertype that works for all subtypes.

Compile-time polymorphism (method overloading): multiple methods same name, different signatures. Resolved at compile time.

Liskov Substitution Principle: Objects of a subclass must be substitutable for objects of the superclass without breaking program correctness.
ch21-3.example:
// Dynamic dispatch example
DECLARE shapes : ARRAY[1:3] OF Shape
shapes[1] ← NEW Circle(5)
shapes[2] ← NEW Rectangle(4, 3)
shapes[3] ← NEW Triangle(6, 4)
FOR i ← 1 TO 3
  OUTPUT shapes[i].Area()   // calls the correct Area() for each actual type
NEXT i

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by dynamic dispatch and why it is useful in OOP.
questions.ms: Method to call is determined at runtime based on the actual object type [1]; allows a variable declared as the supertype to invoke the correct subtype method [1]; enables writing generic code that works with multiple types [1].

ch21-4.title: 21.4 SOLID Principles
ch21-4.subtitle: Five principles for maintainable OOP design

keyTerms.name: Single Responsibility
keyTerms.def: A class should have only one reason to change.

keyTerms.name: Open/Closed
keyTerms.def: Classes open for extension, closed for modification.

keyTerms.name: Liskov Substitution
keyTerms.def: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.

keyTerms.name: Interface Segregation
keyTerms.def: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.

keyTerms.name: Dependency Inversion
keyTerms.def: Depend on abstractions, not concretions.

ch21-4.theory:
Single Responsibility: one class, one job. Reduces coupling and makes classes easier to test.

Open/Closed: use inheritance/interfaces to extend behaviour — no need to modify existing, tested code.

Liskov Substitution: if S is a subtype of T, programs using T should work correctly with S.

Interface Segregation: prefer small, specific interfaces over large, general ones.

Dependency Inversion: high-level modules depend on abstractions (interfaces), not low-level details.
ch21-4.example: Violating SRP: Report class that both formats data AND saves to file. Fix: split into ReportFormatter and ReportSaver.

questions.stem: A class Invoice contains methods: calculateTotal(), printInvoice(), saveToDatabase(). State which SOLID principle this violates and how to fix it.
questions.ms: Violates Single Responsibility Principle [1]; has three reasons to change (calculation logic, printing format, database schema) [1]; fix by splitting into InvoiceCalculator, InvoicePrinter, InvoiceRepository [1].

ch22-1.title: 22.1 Algorithm Complexity and Big-O
ch22-1.subtitle: Analysing time and space efficiency

keyTerms.name: Big-O notation
keyTerms.def: Describes the upper bound of an algorithm's time or space complexity as input size grows.

keyTerms.name: O(1)
keyTerms.def: Constant time — execution time does not depend on input size.

keyTerms.name: O(log n)
keyTerms.def: Logarithmic — input halved each step (e.g., binary search).

keyTerms.name: O(n)
keyTerms.def: Linear — time grows proportionally with input size.

keyTerms.name: O(n²)
keyTerms.def: Quadratic — nested loops over the same data (e.g., bubble sort).

keyTerms.name: Space complexity
keyTerms.def: Memory required by an algorithm as a function of input size.

ch22-1.theory:
Common complexities (best→worst): O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)

How to determine: Count nested loops. One loop → O(n). Loop inside loop → O(n²). Halving input each step → O(log n). Divide and conquer → often O(n log n).

Best/Average/Worst case: Quick sort: best O(n log n), worst O(n²) (sorted array with bad pivot). Binary search: always O(log n).
ch22-1.example:
// O(n²) — bubble sort inner+outer loops
FOR i ← 1 TO n-1
  FOR j ← 1 TO n-i
    IF arr[j] > arr[j+1] THEN swap
NEXT j
NEXT i

questions.stem: State the time complexity of each: (a) binary search, (b) merge sort, (c) linear search, (d) accessing an array by index.
An algorithm has two sequential loops each O(n). State its overall complexity and justify.
questions.ms: O(n) [1]; constants dropped in Big-O notation: O(n) + O(n) = O(2n) → O(n) [1].

ch22-2.title: 22.2 Advanced Sorting: Quicksort and Merge Sort
ch22-2.subtitle: Divide-and-conquer sorting strategies

keyTerms.name: Quicksort
keyTerms.def: Picks a pivot, partitions array around it, recursively sorts sub-arrays.

keyTerms.name: Pivot
keyTerms.def: Element chosen to partition the array; elements < pivot go left, > pivot go right.

keyTerms.name: Merge sort
keyTerms.def: Recursively splits array in half, sorts each half, merges sorted halves.

keyTerms.name: In-place
keyTerms.def: Algorithm that sorts using O(1) extra space (quicksort is in-place; merge sort is not).

keyTerms.name: Stable sort
keyTerms.def: Preserves relative order of equal elements (merge sort is stable; quicksort is not).

ch22-2.theory:
Quicksort steps: Choose pivot → partition (all < pivot left, > pivot right) → recursively sort left and right partitions. Average O(n log n); worst O(n²) when pivot is always min/max.

Merge sort steps: Split until single elements → merge adjacent pairs in sorted order → repeat until fully merged. Always O(n log n) but requires O(n) extra space.

Trade-offs: Quicksort: in-place, cache-friendly but worst case O(n²). Merge sort: guaranteed O(n log n), stable but needs extra memory.
ch22-2.example:
// Merge Sort pseudocode
PROCEDURE MergeSort(arr, left, right)
  IF left < right THEN
    mid ← (left + right) DIV 2
    MergeSort(arr, left, mid)
    MergeSort(arr, mid+1, right)
    Merge(arr, left, mid, right)
  ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

questions.stem: Trace quicksort on [5,1,4,2,8] using the last element as pivot. Show array after each partition.

ch22-3.title: 22.3 Graph Algorithms: BFS, DFS and Dijkstra
ch22-3.subtitle: Traversal and shortest-path algorithms

keyTerms.name: BFS (Breadth-First Search)
keyTerms.def: Explores all neighbours at current depth before moving deeper; uses a queue.

keyTerms.name: DFS (Depth-First Search)
keyTerms.def: Explores as far as possible before backtracking; uses a stack or recursion.

keyTerms.name: Dijkstra's algorithm
keyTerms.def: Finds shortest path from a source to all vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative weights.

keyTerms.name: Relaxation
keyTerms.def: Updating a vertex's tentative distance if a shorter path is found through a neighbour.

keyTerms.name: Priority queue
keyTerms.def: Queue where dequeue returns the item with lowest key; used in Dijkstra's.

ch22-3.theory:
BFS: Start → enqueue → loop: dequeue, visit all unvisited neighbours → enqueue neighbours. Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.

DFS: Start → visit → recurse/push all unvisited neighbours. Can detect cycles; used in topological sort.

Dijkstra's: Initialise all distances to ∞ (source = 0). Repeatedly pick unvisited vertex with smallest distance, relax its edges. Terminates when all vertices visited. Does NOT work with negative edges.
ch22-3.example:
// Dijkstra's trace — A→B(4), A→C(1), C→B(2), B→D(1)
// Initial: A=0, B=∞, C=∞, D=∞
// Visit A: B=4, C=1
// Visit C (dist=1): B=min(4,1+2)=3
// Visit B (dist=3): D=3+1=4
// Visit D (dist=4). Done.
// Shortest: A=0, C=1, B=3, D=4

questions.stem: Explain why Dijkstra's algorithm cannot be used on a graph containing negative edge weights.
questions.ms: Once a vertex is marked as visited/finalised, its distance is not re-examined [1]; a negative edge found later could provide a shorter path to an already-finalised vertex, producing incorrect results [1].

ch22-4.title: 22.4 Dynamic Programming
ch22-4.subtitle: Solving problems by storing sub-problem results

keyTerms.name: Dynamic programming (DP)
keyTerms.def: Solves complex problems by breaking into overlapping sub-problems and storing results (memoisation/tabulation).

keyTerms.name: Memoisation
keyTerms.def: Top-down DP: cache recursive sub-problem results to avoid recomputation.

keyTerms.name: Tabulation
keyTerms.def: Bottom-up DP: fill a table iteratively from base cases to the full problem.

keyTerms.name: Optimal substructure
keyTerms.def: Optimal solution contains optimal solutions to sub-problems.

keyTerms.name: Overlapping sub-problems
keyTerms.def: Same sub-problems are solved repeatedly (unlike divide-and-conquer).

ch22-4.theory:
When to use DP: Problem has optimal substructure AND overlapping sub-problems.

Fibonacci without DP: O(2ⁿ) — exponential. With memoisation: O(n).

Tabulation example (Fibonacci): Build array F[0..n]: F[0]=0, F[1]=1, F[i]=F[i-1]+F[i-2].

Knapsack problem: Classic DP — dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w.
ch22-4.example:
// Tabulation — Fibonacci
FUNCTION FibDP(n : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  DECLARE F : ARRAY[0:n] OF INTEGER
  F[0] ← 0 : F[1] ← 1
  FOR i ← 2 TO n
    F[i] ← F[i-1] + F[i-2]
  NEXT i
  RETURN F[n]
ENDFUNCTION

questions.stem: State the two conditions a problem must satisfy to be solvable by dynamic programming. Give an example of each.
questions.ms: Optimal substructure [1]; e.g. shortest path — sub-paths are also shortest [1]. Overlapping sub-problems [1]; e.g. Fibonacci — F(5) computes F(3) and F(4) which both compute F(2) [1].

ch23-1.title: 23.1 Hash Tables
ch23-1.subtitle: Key-value storage with O(1) average access

keyTerms.name: Hash function
keyTerms.def: Maps a key to an array index (e.g., key MOD tableSize).

keyTerms.name: Collision
keyTerms.def: Two different keys hash to the same index.

keyTerms.name: Chaining
keyTerms.def: Each slot holds a linked list of all entries that hash there.

keyTerms.name: Open addressing
keyTerms.def: On collision, probes alternative slots (linear, quadratic, or double hashing).

keyTerms.name: Load factor
keyTerms.def: Ratio of stored entries to table size; higher load → more collisions.

ch23-1.theory:
Hash function design: Good distribution, fast to compute. Prime table sizes reduce clustering.

Linear probing: Probe slots (h+1), (h+2), … until empty. Simple but causes primary clustering.

Quadratic probing: Probe (h+1²), (h+2²), … Reduces primary clustering but may not probe all slots.

Deletion: With open addressing, cannot simply remove — must mark slot as "deleted" (tombstone) to preserve probe sequences.
ch23-1.example:
// Chain-based lookup
FUNCTION Lookup(key : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
  DECLARE idx : INTEGER
  idx ← HashFn(key) MOD TABLE_SIZE
  DECLARE node : ListNode
  node ← table[idx].head
  WHILE node ≠ NULL DO
    IF node.key = key THEN RETURN node.value ENDIF
    node ← node.next
  ENDWHILE
  RETURN -1  // not found
ENDFUNCTION

questions.stem: Insert keys 14, 17, 27, 9, 4 into a hash table of size 7 using hash(k) = k MOD 7 and linear probing. Show the final table.
questions.ms: 14→0, 17→3, 27→6, 9→2, 4→4 [1 per correct placement, allow error carried forward].

ch23-2.title: 23.2 Trees: AVL and Binary Search Trees
ch23-2.subtitle: Self-balancing trees for efficient search

keyTerms.name: BST property
keyTerms.def: Left child < parent < right child for all nodes.

keyTerms.name: AVL tree
keyTerms.def: Self-balancing BST; height difference between left and right subtrees ≤ 1.

keyTerms.name: Balance factor
keyTerms.def: Height(left subtree) − Height(right subtree); must be −1, 0, or +1 in AVL.

keyTerms.name: Rotation
keyTerms.def: Restructuring operation to restore AVL balance (LL, RR, LR, RL).

keyTerms.name: Height-balanced
keyTerms.def: Tree where all nodes have balance factor in {−1, 0, 1}.

ch23-2.theory:
BST operations: Search/Insert/Delete all O(h) where h = height. Worst case (sorted input) → O(n) linked list.

AVL fix: After insert, walk up tree recalculating balance factors. If |bf| > 1: rotate. LL imbalance → right rotation. RR → left rotation. LR → left-right rotation. RL → right-left rotation.

Benefit: AVL guarantees O(log n) for search/insert/delete.
ch23-2.example:
// Insert 10, 20, 30 into AVL tree
// After 10,20,30: right-heavy (bf=-2 at root)
// Apply left rotation: 20 becomes root
//        20
//       /  //      10   30

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by a rotation in an AVL tree and state when a left rotation is applied.
questions.ms: A rotation restructures nodes to restore the height-balance property [1]; left rotation applied when a node is right-heavy (balance factor = −2) [1] and the right child has balance factor 0 or −1 (right-right case) [1].

ch23-3.title: 23.3 Heaps and Priority Queues
ch23-3.subtitle: Efficient min/max retrieval with complete binary trees

keyTerms.name: Heap
keyTerms.def: Complete binary tree where each node ≥ (max-heap) or ≤ (min-heap) its children.

keyTerms.name: Heapify
keyTerms.def: Process of building or restoring the heap property.

keyTerms.name: Sift-up
keyTerms.def: After insert at end, swap with parent while heap property violated.

keyTerms.name: Sift-down
keyTerms.def: After removing root, move last element to root then swap downward to restore heap.

keyTerms.name: Priority queue
keyTerms.def: ADT where dequeue returns the item with highest/lowest priority; efficiently implemented as a heap.

ch23-3.theory:
Array representation: Root at index 1. For node i: left child = 2i, right child = 2i+1, parent = i DIV 2.

Insert: Append to end → sift-up. O(log n).

Delete max: Replace root with last element → remove last → sift-down. O(log n).

Heap sort: Build max-heap O(n) → repeatedly extract max O(n log n) → total O(n log n), in-place.
ch23-3.example:
// Max-heap sift-down after removing root
// Heap: [_,90,80,70,50,60,30]  →  remove 90
// Move 30 to root: [_,30,80,70,50,60]
// Sift-down: 30<80, swap → [_,80,30,70,50,60]
// 30<50, swap → [_,80,50,70,30,60]  (stable)

questions.stem: Given min-heap [5,10,8,15,20], insert the value 3. Show each swap during sift-up.

ch24-1.title: 24.1 Cryptographic Techniques
ch24-1.subtitle: Symmetric, asymmetric and hashing schemes

keyTerms.name: Symmetric encryption
keyTerms.def: Same key used for encryption and decryption (e.g., AES).

keyTerms.name: Asymmetric encryption
keyTerms.def: Public key encrypts; private key decrypts (or vice versa for signing). E.g., RSA.

keyTerms.name: Public key
keyTerms.def: Shared openly; used to encrypt messages sent to the key owner.

keyTerms.name: Private key
keyTerms.def: Kept secret; used to decrypt messages or create digital signatures.

keyTerms.name: Hashing
keyTerms.def: One-way function producing fixed-length digest; cannot be reversed.

keyTerms.name: Digital signature
keyTerms.def: Hash of message encrypted with sender's private key; verifies authenticity and integrity.

ch24-1.theory:
Symmetric encryption: Fast; problem is secure key exchange. Used for bulk data (AES-256).

Asymmetric encryption: Solves key distribution — public key shared freely. Slower. RSA widely used.

Hybrid encryption: TLS/HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption to exchange a session key, then symmetric for speed.

Digital signatures: Alice signs with private key → Bob verifies with Alice's public key. Provides non-repudiation.

Hash functions (SHA-256): deterministic, fast, avalanche effect (small input change → completely different hash), collision-resistant.
ch24-1.example:
HTTPS handshake summary:

  1. Client sends supported cipher suites.
  2. Server sends certificate (contains public key).
  3. Client verifies certificate via CA.
  4. Client generates session key, encrypts with server's public key, sends.
  5. Server decrypts with private key; both now have shared session key.
  6. Remaining communication uses symmetric encryption with session key.

questions.stem: Explain the role of a Certificate Authority (CA) in HTTPS.
questions.ms: CA is a trusted third party [1]; digitally signs the server's certificate confirming the public key belongs to the claimed domain [1]; client verifies the CA's signature using the CA's public key (pre-installed in browser/OS) to authenticate the server [1].

ch24-2.title: 24.2 Network Security Threats and Defences
ch24-2.subtitle: Attacks, vulnerabilities and countermeasures

keyTerms.name: SQL injection
keyTerms.def: Inserting malicious SQL into input fields to manipulate database queries.

keyTerms.name: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
keyTerms.def: Injecting malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users.

keyTerms.name: DDoS
keyTerms.def: Distributed Denial of Service — overwhelming a server with traffic from many sources.

keyTerms.name: Firewall
keyTerms.def: Filters network traffic by IP, port, and protocol; blocks unauthorised access.

keyTerms.name: Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
keyTerms.def: Monitors network traffic for suspicious patterns and alerts administrators.

ch24-2.theory:
SQL injection prevention: Parameterised queries (prepared statements), input validation, principle of least privilege for DB accounts.

XSS prevention: Escape HTML special characters in output; Content Security Policy headers; HTTPOnly cookies.

Defence in depth: Multiple layers — firewall, IDS, encryption, authentication, access control. A breach of one layer is mitigated by others.
ch24-2.example:
// Vulnerable SQL:
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'"
// If input = "'; DROP TABLE users; --" → catastrophic

// Fixed (parameterised):
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
execute(query, [input])

questions.stem: Describe how SQL injection works and state two methods to prevent it.
questions.ms: Attacker inputs SQL code into a form field [1]; unvalidated input incorporated into query changes its meaning [1]. Prevention: parameterised queries/prepared statements [1]; input validation/sanitisation OR whitelist acceptable characters [1].

ch24-3.title: 24.3 Privacy, Ethics and Legislation
ch24-3.subtitle: Legal and ethical dimensions of computing

keyTerms.name: Data Protection Act
keyTerms.def: UK legislation requiring lawful, fair, transparent data processing with clear purpose and user rights.

keyTerms.name: GDPR
keyTerms.def: EU General Data Protection Regulation — strict rules on consent, data minimisation, right to erasure.

keyTerms.name: Privacy by design
keyTerms.def: Embedding privacy protections into systems from the start, not as an afterthought.

keyTerms.name: Intellectual property
keyTerms.def: Legal right over creative works; includes copyright, patents, trademarks.

keyTerms.name: Whistleblowing
keyTerms.def: Exposing illegal or unethical practices by an organisation; legal protections vary by jurisdiction.

ch24-3.theory:
Key data protection principles: Lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality.

Ethical frameworks: Consequentialism (judge by outcomes), Deontology (duty-based rules), Virtue ethics (character). Exam questions often ask you to present both sides and reach a justified conclusion.

Computer Misuse Act 1990 (UK): Unauthorised access, unauthorised access with intent, unauthorised modification of computer material.
ch24-3.example:
Scenario: A company stores customer passwords in plain text. Evaluate ethically:

  • Against: Violates users' right to privacy/security; data breach exposes passwords; negligent storage.
  • For: (none defensible — this is unambiguously poor practice)
  • GDPR angle: Violates integrity/confidentiality principle; DPA breach.

questions.stem: A developer proposes storing user passwords as MD5 hashes. Discuss whether this is adequate from a security perspective.
questions.ms: MD5 is a hash so passwords not stored plaintext [1]; however MD5 is cryptographically broken / fast to compute [1]; rainbow table / brute-force attacks feasible [1]; should use bcrypt/Argon2 with salt instead [1].

ch25-1.title: 25.1 Functional Programming Concepts
ch25-1.subtitle: Declarative programming with pure functions and higher-order functions

keyTerms.name: Pure function
keyTerms.def: Function with no side effects; same input always produces same output.

keyTerms.name: Immutability
keyTerms.def: Data cannot be changed after creation; new values computed from old ones.

keyTerms.name: Higher-order function
keyTerms.def: Function that takes another function as argument or returns a function.

keyTerms.name: Map
keyTerms.def: Applies a function to every element of a list, returning a new list.

keyTerms.name: Filter
keyTerms.def: Returns a new list containing only elements satisfying a predicate.

keyTerms.name: Fold/Reduce
keyTerms.def: Combines list elements using a function and an accumulator into a single value.

ch25-1.theory:
Functional vs imperative: Functional programs describe what to compute; imperative programs describe how.

Benefits: Easier reasoning about code, no shared state bugs, natural parallelism, easier testing (pure functions).

Lambda (anonymous) functions: Functions defined inline without a name — x → x * x.

Closure: Function that captures variables from its enclosing scope.
ch25-1.example:
// Pseudocode approximation
// Map: square each element
result ← map(x → x*x, [1,2,3,4])  // [1,4,9,16]

// Filter: keep only even numbers
evens ← filter(x → x MOD 2 = 0, [1,2,3,4,5])  // [2,4]

// Fold: sum all elements
total ← fold((acc,x) → acc+x, 0, [1,2,3,4])  // 10

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a pure function and a function with side effects. Give an example of each.
questions.ms: Pure function: returns same output for same input, no observable side effects [1]; example: square(x) returns x² [1]. Side-effect function: modifies external state / performs I/O [1]; example: procedure that writes to a file or updates a global variable [1].

ch25-2.title: 25.2 Declarative Programming and Logic
ch25-2.subtitle: Prolog-style facts, rules and queries

keyTerms.name: Fact
keyTerms.def: A basic assertion that is always true (e.g., parent(tom, bob).)

keyTerms.name: Rule
keyTerms.def: A conditional statement: head :- body (head is true if body is true).

keyTerms.name: Query
keyTerms.def: A question posed to the logic database; interpreter searches for a satisfying binding.

keyTerms.name: Unification
keyTerms.def: Process of matching variables to values to make a goal true.

keyTerms.name: Backtracking
keyTerms.def: Returning to a previous choice point when current path fails to find a solution.

ch25-2.theory:
Prolog execution: Interpreter attempts to satisfy goals left-to-right; if a goal fails, it backtracks to the last choice point and tries an alternative.

Sample facts and rules:

parent(tom, bob).
parent(tom, liz).
grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).

Query: grandparent(tom, Who)? → Who = bob; Who = liz.

Negation as failure: not(Goal) succeeds if Goal cannot be proved.
ch25-2.example:
// Ancestral rules
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), ancestor(Z, Y).

// Query: ancestor(tom, liz)?
// → parent(tom, liz) → TRUE

questions.stem: Given facts: parent(ann,bob). parent(bob,cal). Rule: ancestor(X,Y):-parent(X,Y). ancestor(X,Y):-parent(X,Z),ancestor(Z,Y). Trace how ancestor(ann,cal) is proved.
questions.ms: Try first clause: parent(ann,cal) — fails [1]; try second clause: parent(ann,Z) → Z=bob [1]; prove ancestor(bob,cal) → try first: parent(bob,cal) → succeeds [1]; goal proved [1].

ch25-3.title: 25.3 Low-Level and Assembly Programming
ch25-3.subtitle: Registers, instruction sets and assembly translation

keyTerms.name: Instruction set
keyTerms.def: Complete set of machine instructions a processor can execute.

keyTerms.name: Register
keyTerms.def: Small, fast storage location within the CPU (ACC, IX, PC, MAR, MDR, CIR).

keyTerms.name: Addressing mode
keyTerms.def: How an instruction's operand is interpreted: immediate, direct, indirect, indexed.

keyTerms.name: Immediate addressing
keyTerms.def: Operand is the actual value (e.g., LDM #5 loads 5 into ACC).

keyTerms.name: Direct addressing
keyTerms.def: Operand is a memory address (e.g., LDD 200 loads value at address 200).

keyTerms.name: Indexed addressing
keyTerms.def: Effective address = operand + index register IX.

ch25-3.theory:
Cambridge 9618 assembly subset:

LDM #nLoad immediate value n into ACC
LDD addrLoad from memory address into ACC
STO addrStore ACC to memory address
ADD addrACC ← ACC + [addr]
CMP #n / addrCompare ACC with value; set flags
JPN labelJump if negative flag set
ENDHalt program
ch25-3.example:
// Pseudocode: x ← 5 + y
LDM #5    // ACC = 5
ADD yAddr // ACC = 5 + y
STO xAddr // x = ACC
END

questions.stem: Translate to assembly: IF x > 10 THEN y ← 0 ELSE y ← 1. Use registers ACC and addresses Ax (for x) and Ay (for y).
questions.ms: LDD Ax [1]; CMP #10 [1]; JPN else_label [1]; LDM #0 STO Ay [branch to end] [1]; else_label: LDM #1 STO Ay [1].

ch25-4.title: 25.4 Compiler Stages and Language Translation
ch25-4.subtitle: How source code becomes machine code

keyTerms.name: Lexical analysis
keyTerms.def: Tokenises source code — removes whitespace/comments, produces token stream.

keyTerms.name: Syntax analysis (parsing)
keyTerms.def: Checks token stream against grammar rules; builds parse tree / AST.

keyTerms.name: Semantic analysis
keyTerms.def: Checks meaning: type checking, scope resolution, undeclared variable detection.

keyTerms.name: Code generation
keyTerms.def: Converts intermediate representation to target machine code or bytecode.

keyTerms.name: Optimisation
keyTerms.def: Improves generated code for speed/size: constant folding, dead code elimination, loop unrolling.

keyTerms.name: Interpreter
keyTerms.def: Executes source code directly without producing machine code; no separate compile step.

ch25-4.theory:
Compilation stages: Source → [Lexer] → Tokens → [Parser] → AST → [Semantic Analysis] → Annotated AST → [Code Generator] → Machine Code → [Linker] → Executable.

Compiler vs Interpreter: Compiler translates whole program once → faster execution. Interpreter translates line by line → slower but easier debugging and cross-platform.

Bytecode / JIT: Java/Python compile to bytecode (intermediate), then JIT compiles hot paths to native code at runtime — combines portability and speed.
ch25-4.example:
// Lexical analysis of:  x := 5 + y
// Tokens: [ID:"x"] [OP:":="] [INT:5] [OP:"+"] [ID:"y"]

// Parse tree:
//   AssignStmt
//   ├── ID: x
//   └── AddExpr
//       ├── INT: 5
//       └── ID: y

questions.stem: Describe the role of the lexical analyser and the semantic analyser in a compiler. Give one error each stage would detect.
questions.ms: Lexical: tokenises source; detects invalid characters / unrecognised symbols [2]. Semantic: checks meaning — type checking, scope resolution; detects type mismatch (adding string to integer) / use of undeclared variable [2].
